speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. On December 2, when replying to a question asking whether guidelines for Canadian Crown corporations and other corporations owned by the government exist, the Prime Minister said such guidelines do exist. He went on to say that they contained instructions from ministers to the corporations under their responsi-

February 10, 1977

bility. Considering that, according to the Polysar report of January 31, of this year, PISA, the subsidiary of Polysar, continued with kickback practices at least until September 1976 and conceivably beyond that point, would the Prime Minister explain what steps were taken to enforce the guidelines to which he referred on December 2?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENFORCE GUIDELINES FOR CONDUCT OF POLYSAR AND OTHER CROWN CORPORATIONS

I do not have before me that text of the exchanges between the hon. member and myself, but I have quite an accurate memory of the exchange and I remember indicating that there were corporations and departments which did have guidelines. I certainly did not say they all had. I had in mind certain Crown corporations and agencies. One example I had in mind was the Canadian Commercial Corporation. I went on to say that we were going to issue over-all guidelines which would apply to all departments, agencies and Crown corporations, and we did that a couple of weeks later. Until then there had been no formal guidelines applying to all.
I did indicate that it was the duty of every government agent and corporation to act within the law and the confines of morality. But the precise guidelines spelling that out in detail and applicable to all were made public by the President of the Treasury Board around mid-December.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENFORCE GUIDELINES FOR CONDUCT OF POLYSAR AND OTHER CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext: Since in his answer of December 2 the Prime Minister did make specific reference to the fact that ministers who had Crown corporations under their jurisdiction did in fact have such guidelines and did in fact pass them on to the corporations under their reponsibility, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he has confirmed that such specific guidelines did apply and were made clear to the Polymer corporation, which was the name by which it was known at the time of the Auditor General's report of 1973, and subsequent to that time, particularly since the matter was raised in the House last fall. Did the Prime Minister take steps to ensure that all Crown corporations received very explicit guidelines that covered these matters?

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ACTION TO ENFORCE GUIDELINES FOR CONDUCT OF POLYSAR AND OTHER CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
The answer to the final part of the question is very clear. We did take such steps and we enunciated the guidelines in the House in mid-December. As far as the first part of the question is concerned, it repeats the earlier one and I repeat my earlier reply. This whole matter of guidelines for the conduct of Crown corporations was discussed by me with certain of the ministers and some of them said that they followed some practices of having guidelines within the departments, and that is what I said.
I did not indicate that every department, agency and Crown corporation was submitted to them. If that had been the case, indeed there would have been no need in mid-December to issue general guidelines. The Minister of Supply and Services, following this exchange or perhaps even preceding it, asked a group of cabinet ministers to put these guidelines in shape and he and the President of the Treasury Board co-operated in

establishing guidelines which would apply to all. Those were the ones that were enunciated in the House.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF GOVERNMENT AUDIT OF CROWN AGENCIES AND INVESTIGATION OF MANAGEMENT STRUCTURE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. For the past few years ministers have been asking this type of question about Crown corporations, not so much relating to the legality or morality of their actions but to the degree of control the government has over every aspect of their actions. It has been a dilemma which comes up under many circumstances. For example, when a Crown corporation does not carry out the objectives of the people of Canada what can we do about it? When a Crown corporation has budgets which are very often approved by the government but we are without the ability to go into the details of the management, what can we do about it? We have studied various possible answers to these questions, one of them being to give the government the power of direction- either broad direction to the Crown corporation or specific direction.
This whole matter has been before us and even though we have studied the practices in other countries, we find it difficult to arrive at a solution which would be entirely acceptable to the House of Commons and to the traditions in Canada where Crown corporations are indeed at arm's length and where the "politicians" should not be giving specific direction and intervening in the operation.
This is the dilemma we are struggling with, and I think in the Air Canada Act which is before the House now we have indicated some of the directions in which we are trying to solve this by giving the government specific authority to issue directives of a general nature to Crown corporations. I have no clear statement or final statement, however, in answer to the hon. member's preoccupation which we share on this side.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
That this House denounces the government's failure to generate jobs in Canada, particularly in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, and urges immediate and resolute action, including the early presentation of a budget.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion we shall debate today which stands in my name is inspired by the most recent unemployment figures announced earlier this week which shocked all members of the House. They are shocking not simply in terms of the human burden which they impose on nearly one million Canadians who are out of work, but they are also disturbing by reason of what they say about our capacity to keep our country together and realize the economic growth potential which exists here and which can be one of the central means of ensuring that Canadians will choose, because it makes economic and other sense for them so to choose, to remain part of a large country full of promise and possibility.
I do not intend to dwell at length on the figures which are all too familiar to the House of Commons and to those upon whom they impact most directly. To make the House clearly aware of the degree of the problem we are facing, it would be helpful to enter on the record some relevant figures. Last month the number of unemployed in Canada, according to Statistics Canada, reached 889,000. That, sir, is the highest figure recorded by that agency in the more than 20 years it has been providing this labour force survey.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Shocking.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
These are shocking figures, a shocking way in which to start the year 1977, and present a great challenge to the country. The number of people who were actually working in January, even on a seasonally adjusted basis, was up only 70,000 from one year earlier, while the labour force had increased by more than 150,000. That means that in 1976 we created new jobs for less than half the new entrants to the Canadian labour force. While we were registering that meagre performance, we made no progress at all in reducing the backlog of jobless in this country.
Unemployment in the five eastern provinces of Canada- Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island-was even more serious because the number of jobs available there was down by 24,000 from one year ago. During 1976, fully 50 per cent of the increase in

unemployment occurred in the province of Quebec. I repeat, 50 per cent occurred in that one province. Thirty per cent of it was accounted for by the Atlantic provinces. That is, eight out of every ten Canadians who joined the ranks of the unemployed in 1976 lived in those five eastern provinces of Canada.
On a longer term basis it is worth noting that over the past decade the unemployment rate for Atlantic Canada has been, on average, 50 per cent higher than for the country as a whole. In Quebec, the average rate during those ten years of the life of the present government has run at 30 per cent above the figure for Canada as a whole.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Some government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
The aspect of those figures which is most troubling is that among young people-among those in the 15 to 24 age group-the rate of unemployment in Canada in January was 15.2 per cent, or close to double the figure for the labour force as a whole. The figure with respect to young people in Quebec was 17 per cent. That is to say, the unemployment figure was 17 per cent and in Newfoundland it was as high as 29 per cent. That was the figure applying to those who were forced by the economic policies of this government to begin their work career without the possibility of finding a job.
One could go on at great length enumerating this dismal catalogue. I want to go on and recite one or two basic factors. First, unemployment has been rising in Canada even though one of our traditional excuses, the old boast about having the fastest growing labour force in the western world, no longer rings true. It does not hold water any more. In fact, our work force grew last year at less than half the rate experienced by the United States. It is important to note that in the United States the unemployment rate has been moving steadily downward, while in this country it has been creeping steadily upward. Second, the so-called participation rate, the number of eligible Canadians actually in the work force, is down over one year ago, otherwise our problems would be even worse than they actually are.
Finally, I think it is important as we consider this question to take note of the forecasts of the Conference Board. They say that without some action by this government to stimulate growth and generate jobs, unemployment will average more than 10 per cent this year in all the five eastern provinces which have already borne the brunt of unemployment brought on by the economic policies of this government. We are speaking not simply about figures to feed to computers; we are talking about individual Canadians, about people who face the fundamental problem of obtaining a job around which they can build their lives and on which they can base their futures. We are dealing here not just with a passing event, not with a statistic which cropped up this month and is going to pass away, but with what has become an unfortunate feature of life in Canada under this government and one which has a very permanent and dangerous impact upon the lives not only of individual Canadians but upon our capacity to grow together as a country.
February 10, 1977

I want to read to the House of Commons excerpts from a letter that was sent originally to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) from a man in Victoria. He received no answer from the Prime Minister's office and so sent the correspondence to me. In a long and eloquent letter he talks about his six children; his oldest son, having worked his way through university, now unable to find a job in his profession; his daughter, a graduate nurse, in the same predicament; his daughter's boy friend, with a degree in business administration, also not able to find a job. The example, he says, is discouraging to his younger children. One of his daughters is talking about going to work in a fish plant in British Columbia when she graduates from high school because "when they are open she can earn great money", and because it is seasonal work she can draw UIC benefits when the fish plant is closed. That will give her time, she says, to walk on the beach and sit in a beer parlour with hundreds of other kids planning a similar future. This father asks:
What the hell is wrong? Why are we letting this happen to us?
He concludes:
I think everyone owes their country a service. I also happen to believe that a country owes something to its citizens, especially the ones that are working and striving to be better citizens and are preparing themselves to do great things. They've got to have a chance or we are finished.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: That is the report of one father, of one correspondent, to one member of parliament. Colleagues on this side of the House can cite countless others, particular those who come from regions of the country where unemployment has hit hardest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hundreds of them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
The point, which is an important one to make, relates to what has been called the work ethic in Canada. Sometimes the suggestion is made that Canadians generally, and young Canadians in particular, do not want to work, that that is the reason they, in the words of this father, walk on the beach and sit in the beer parlours. There have been studies by this very government of the extent to which the work ethic is strong in Canada and the conclusions are that the work ethic is alive and well in Canada if there is work for those who practise that ethic.
I want to read into the record excerpts from Canadian Work Values prepared by the Department of Manpower and Immigration relating to surveys conducted over the last two years. It reads:
When those in the labour force were asked whether they would rather-if given their preference-work full-time, part-time or never, more than 95 per cent chose either full-time or part-time.
Later the report reads:
Seventy-five percent of those people who said they were in the labour force agreed that "I work more because I like to than because I have to".
Those are not reports of a country in which the work ethic is in trouble or is in decline. The cause of the unemployment
Unemployment
figures that we have seen this month is not based upon the failure of the work ethic but, instead, on the failure of the government of Canada to recognize its responsibility.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
The matter which has to concern us most as parliamentarians planning the future of this country is that while the work ethic is alive and well in Canada, Canadians like other people, are very adaptable. If our institutions create situations where there are no jobs to go to, where it is easier to go on unemployment insurance and to walk the beaches and stay in the beer parlours than it is to find work, then we will see a decline in that work ethic, not because there is a decline in the will of young Canadians but because this government is not doing its job of giving Canadians a chance. There is no question in my mind that this government can break down the Canadian work ethic if it wants to, and it gives every indication of it by its failure to generate jobs.
There are other long-term political impacts to the kind of statistics that we saw the other day. One of them clearly relates to political stability in this country, because there is a clear relationship between political stability and economic progress even in this fortunate country.

Let us take the case of the province of Quebec, for example. It would be easy to delude ourselves and believe that a few cultural concessions will solve all our problems and consequently that the threat of separatism will vanish forever. Nothing could be further from the truth.
I had the opportunity, both before and after my election as leader of the Progressive Conservative party, to visit the various regions of this province and each time I saw that Quebeckers attach great importance to the economic well being of their province. The federal government seems to be the only one to ignore it. Nevertheless, last November 15, when they brought the Parti Quebecois to power, the people of Quebec expressed their economical concerns in no uncertain terms. I have already said, and I repeat it today, that Quebeckers did not vote in favour of independence, but for an efficient government likely to grapple with and solve the very concrete problems they are facing. Unemployment is surely one of those problems.
In that context the federal government must of course assume its share of responsibilities, urgently face reality and introduce real solutions to the unemployment problem, not just palliatives. If it remains apathetic, it will only emphasize the risk of making part of the population lose all hope and opt for radical solutions.

Mr. Speaker, there is also a third long-term impact of this continuing slowness of growth, this continuing failure to realize the promise of the country. That is the development of a sense in Canada that we are a stagnant country, not achieving the growth of which we are capable, not generating the jobs which our young people and other Canadians have a right to
80008-471/2

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
expect, not realizing a potential which is unparallelled among the nations of the world if only our government would act to achieve that potential.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
The sense of stagnation that is developing in the country also imposes strains upon our unity as a nation. There is now, in western Canada, growing talk in loud voices, with perhaps few numbers behind them at the moment, about a kind of separatism in that region. I think it is important for us to recognize that where part of the sense of separatism in the eastern provinces is separatism of the disadvantaged, what we are seeing in western Canada right now is, instead, separatism flowing from the frustration of the entrepreneur. This frustration is flowing from people who sense that their country is being stacked against them, is placing obstacles in the path of the generation of growth and the generation of jobs which is so much part of the ethic of that region.
We are not talking here simply about the statistics which came from Statistics Canada the other day. We are talking about human lives, human opportunities and about serious impacts upon our capacity as a nation to grow together, to remain together and to maintain the work ethic and the standards which have been part of the Canadian experience and have generated the growth and the progress that we have known in this country. The government can no longer blame external circumstances or other governments, the opposition or anybody else, because they have been the government of Canada for nearly a decade and some of their ministers have been in office longer than that. They are clearly responsible for the failure of this country to realize the economic growth potential and generate the jobs that we can in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
I am not going to detain or entertain the House today with a long review of the record of bad government we have received from the government opposite. It is all too well known to Canadians. However, it is important to remember in passing that one justification this government gave for introducing a controls program by surprise, in the dead of the night and without consultation, was that that would allow the government to avoid fighting inflation by recession and unemployment. Now, as a result of the mismanagement of the affairs of this country by the government, we have the worst of both worlds. We have a system of controls, with all its distortions in investment patterns, in loss of new plants, in loss of new jobs and in diversion of opportunity to other countries or to other times, and we also have a situation of near recession. We have an economy which underperformed its realistic growth potential last year, and unless some definite action is taken by this government it is going to do even worse this year.
Yet the minister tells us, in effect, that his hands are tied and he cannot do anything to get the economy back on a course of sound and steady economic growth, because if he does, he might overstimulate it. 1 ask the minister, and

Canadians also ask him: is he not aware of the amount of slack which already exists in this economy? Does he not feel that there is considerable room for stimulation in an economy which has unused capacity of up to 20 per cent in some sectors? How can he be so afraid of overstimulation when the Conference Board forecasts that without some change in government policy we will have negative real capital investment in 1977?
I want to talk for a moment about the argument of unused capacity because it is interesting in that regard to look at some of the figures for the third quarter of 1976, figures on the utilization of productive capacity in manufacturing industries, industries which would create jobs if encouragement were given to them. The figures show that during the last three months of 1976 the chemical industry was operating at only 83 per cent of its established capacity. I remind the House that furniture producers, heavily active in the province of Quebec, were employing only 72 per cent of their productive capacity. The electrical products industry was operating at 81 per cent capacity, and the durable goods sector-automobiles, major appliances and the like-was functioning at 82 per cent capacity. What is significant here is not simply the failure to come closer to capacity; it is that many of the industries which have been operating at less than capacity are in those parts of Canada where the unemployment problem we have today is most acute.
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald)-I hope he takes the opportunity today-has an obligation to explain to the House why the President of the United States feels justified in advocating some $30 billion in new stimulus for the economy of the United States, which already is an economy outperforming ours in every major category. Why is it that the Carter administration feels that it can and, indeed, that it must provide stimulation to the U.S. economy, which is already growing faster than ours, at a time when unemployment in the U.S. is going down, and yet we cannot act in an economy which it is forecast will grow no more than 3.5 per cent this year and at a time when unemployment threatens to reach one million Canadians? I would be interested in hearing the minister's answer to that question. There is one answer which is well known on this side, and it is that, unlike the government of Canada, the government of the United States is committed to providing jobs for its citizens. That is a model and an example which should be followed here.
There are a number of matters which one might want to touch upon today, but I think one of the fundamental requirements is a new budget as soon as possible. Today the Minister of Finance indicated that there might be one before Easter. The other day in the House he spoke in terms of several months from now. Canadians rely upon economic growth and upon the generation of jobs and they just cannot wait for the convenience of the Minister of Finance. We need a budget as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
February 10, 1977

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
Just in case the reason for the minister's delay is that he does not know what to do, we want to take the opportunity today to suggest some of the elements which that budget should contain, elements which would cut into the recurrent high unemployment figures in this country and which would give Canadians not only a chance but a sense of having a chance in this country.

First, in the budget it should be recognized that permanent employment is created not by government programs but rather by strong economic expansion in the private sector.
Second, steps must be taken to encourage consumer demand, perhaps by reducing sales tax: this would not create inflation.
Third, activity in the field of housing in Canada is slowing down at an alarming rate, at a time when the jobs in that industry are most necessary. That slowing down is particularly obvious in the construction of new units, the sector where the rate of vacancies is the lowest.
Stimulants must therefore be found to give new momentum in that field. If need be, the minister should say he is willing to discuss with the provinces the impact of rent controls in new buildings.
Fourth, we have witnessed in Canada for some time now serious cuts, on the part of corporations, in their budgets for research and development. These cannot be gauged strictly in terms of lost jobs. They are also contributing to our loss of competitiveness in foreign markets. Adequate stimulants are needed to encourage new expenditures in R and D, of such a nature as to encourage innovation and industrial productivity.
Fifth, the government should seriously consider introducing the concept of special fiscal contracts with companies desirous of locating new industries in underdeveloped areas of our country.
This approach which was applied with a certain amount of success in the Republic of Ireland and in New Hampshire in the United States has more guarantees to offer, I think, than the various measures put forward by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, as far as a viable and continuous industrial development in these areas is concerned. Mr. Speaker, to anyone who has the courage to face reality, it is clear that Canada has to cope with a serious problem: the lack of confidence on the part of investors.
This lack of confidence does not solely issue from the results of the November 15 election in Quebec, and I insist on this point. At most, the election of a new government in Quebec added a new element of uncertainty to an already precarious situation. On this point, it should be noted that, according to the Conference Board, new capital investments in Canada will drop this year and that this forecast is based on data which were compiled before the election in Quebec.

It is worth noting, too, that the Atlantic Economic Council has been pointing to this problem for some time as a major element behind the continuing difficulties in that region. It is
Unemployment
time-indeed, past time-that the government of Canada faced up to this problem squarely and honestly. It is not going to help the situation one iota for ministers to begin, as some of them have already begun, at least by insinuation, to try to shift the blame for the problem to the new government of the province of Quebec rather than to the policies of the government of Canada. If investors have any concern about the future course of political events in Quebec, that is all the more reason for their being able to look to the federal government with some sense of confidence and some sense of reassurance.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
So if it has been important for the government of Canada to create a climate of confidence in this country prior to this point, it is even more important now. That sense of confidence has been sadly missing for far too long. When we needed a climate of certainty we had a government that consistently changed the rules, often in the middle of the night and often without warning or, just as bad, a government that left important sectors of the economy hanging for years with no rules at all. Perhaps when one looks at all this, the difference in the approach of the two principal parties in the country to the economic future of the country and our capacity to create jobs and realize our potential, in the final analysis it comes down to a basic view of this country.
The Prime Minister and this government talk a lot about the virtues of Canada and why Canadians in all parts of the country want to keep it together. I do not doubt for one moment their dedication to the principle of unity. Of course they are committed to it, as all of us are committed to it. But the more I see of this government, the more I watch and hear their responses to the critical problems of Canada, the more I am struck by how little they really expect of Canada and how small and narrow a vision of this country they offer to Canadians.
That small vision makes it easy for them virtually to ignore the 800,000 jobless. They do not seem to believe Canada can do any better than that. This is a government which offers no real hope to Canadians, because it has no real hope itself. If there is any danger that Canadians are uncaring about the unemployed and the underemployed among us-and I do not believe Canadians are uncaring-it is partly because they have a federal government that does not seem to care.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
We have been given a great gift in this country-a gift of potential to grow, to find opportunities, to express ourselves, to build secure lives, to build good families. This is a country whose potential is literally unparallelled in the world-a country of great promise. The sadness is that we are not realizing the potential for growth, for jobs or for progress. Instead, we have a country dominated by unemployment, by anger and by a growing sense of despair.

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
In a speech the Prime Minister made recently outside the House he indicated some fundamental changes in the rigid approach to federalism that has marked the government's conduct in the past. We have yet to see the proof of that promise although it has been made. I take the occasion of introducing this motion to make the point clear that we need from this government, immediately, an indication that it is prepared fundamentally to change its approach to economic progress in this country. We have been stagnant too long. We have a country to build. We have jobs to encourage. We have great promise to achieve. It will not be done by the timid policies of this government. It will only be done if there is determination to realize the potential of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party to give our unqualified support to the motion before the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
I do so because since this parliament returned last fall after the summer recess we have been saying that the number one issue before Canada, both in economic and human terms-and not just the people of Atlantic Canada or Quebec, as important as their problems are-is that of unemployment. Although the official figures published within the last couple of days indicate that 889,000 people are unemployed, for reasons that I and other members of my party have tried to make clear in recent days the accurate figure realistically describing the number of Canadians out of work is over one million. That is the highest level of unemployment not only since Statistics Canada has been providing data but since the depression. Politicians frequently indulge in rhetoric that causes language to lose its original meaning, but in this case we have what can only be appropriately described as a human tragedy for over one million Canadians.
We support the motion because we believe it is a fundamental objective of any government at the national or provincial level to create opportunities for work. If there is anything which my party and I stand for in global terms-I refer to the social democratic movement-it is the opportunity within the framework of the economy of any country for men and women who want to work to do so. People in Canada, as elsewhere, want jobs; they do not want hand-outs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
After all kinds of pressure-indeed, 1 am prepared to acknowledge pressure within their own ranks- this government created an unemployment insurance system that is good. What it has not done is to provide the complement that social democratic parties have always done-assurance of the possibility of work. If you have a social insurance scheme that enables people to live with dignity when they are out of work, the absolutely essential concomitant to that is a commitment to full employment to minimize the number of jobs at any time without occupants. It has been the total failure of this government to consider that option that is so objectionable and so fundamentally distasteful to anyone who

is concerned. Human dignity can only come to individuals and their families from the capacity and opportunity to work, to contribute to their families and to the community through productive labour.
We believe in the motion basically because of our commitment to the right, as we see it, of all Canadians to have a job and an opportunity to make their contribution. We are, and have been, concerned about the direction of this government because of its mishandling of the economy leading to serious negative consequences for the country. If more of the 93 per cent of the people who have jobs are not as concerned as we would like about creating opportunities for those without work, at least they should be concerned about the immense cost of this level of unemployment to the economy and they should be moved by the economic arguments. In 1972, $1.9 billion was paid in unemployment insurance benefits; in 1975, the figure was $3.1 billion.
If you compare the first nine months of 1975 of unemployment insurance pay-outs with the first nine months of 1976, which is the most recent figure available, we see that in 1976 we were running well ahead of 1975 in terms of what it was going to cost in unemployment insurance pay-outs for people to do nothing. In the first nine months of 1975 it cost Canadians $2.6 billion in unemployment insurance pay-outs. In the comparable period of 1976 it cost $2.8 billion-up .2 per cent. There can be no doubt that when the final figures are in for 1976 we will have spent more than ever before in Canadian history on unemployment insurance pay-outs to people who need and deserve the money. There should be no mistake about that. If people cannot have the opportunity to work, we must ensure they have the economic subsistence to get by. My point is that it is an immensely stupid drain on the economy to pay people to do nothing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
Second, if you calculate the lost production in goods and services which we would have had if these men and women had been working, it costs the Canadian economy about $6 billion a year. That would go a considerable way toward reducing the rate of inflation. Increasing the supply of goods and services, as every economist knows, would have the effect of bringing down prices. We are losing that production. Finally, in terms of economic costs we are losing hundreds of millions of dollars in tax revenues that these men and women would be paying if they were employed. Because they are not employed, and therefore not paying the level of tax they would pay if they had jobs, other working Canadians have to bear a disproportionate share of the tax burden. In addition to the human costs which are fundamental to us, the economic costs to the Canadian economy in billions of dollars year after year should cause all Canadians to be concerned about this question. It should motivate even this sterile government to take some concrete steps to turn the economy around.
February 10, 1977

The phenomenon we are dealing with is not a recent one. It is important for us to absorb that fact. It is not a new practice of the Liberal government. In fact, it is not just characteristic of that party. The last time we had comparable levels of unemployment, although they were not quite as bad, was during the last years of a Tory government. In the period 1962-63, unemployment figures were setting new levels of undesirableness for the Canadian economy. What I am saying is that this pattern is characteristic of parties in this country which have governed at the national level. They do not believe in taking the steps that are required in terms of national economic planning to deal with both unemployment and inflation.
Mir. Stevens: Like in the United Kingdom.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext: Like the socialists in the U.K. Tell us what is happening in England.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
1 am hearing examples of governments trying to clean up decades of Tory mess. They are trying to clean up decades of Tory mismanagement. Listen to the statistics. I will give the figures for the United Kingdom and a few other countries. Here is the record, comparative terms, of the eight leading industrial countries. These are the average unemployment figures for the period 1960 to 1974. The best is West Germany, which has had a social democratic government for years, with an average of .8 per cent. The next is Japan, with 1.3 per cent. I give credit to Japan because they believe in some economic planning, unlike the Tories to my right or the Liberals across the way. Third is Sweden, with 1.9 per cent. Fourth is France, with a 2.3 per cent average. Then the United Kingdom, with a 3.2 per cent average; Italy, with a 3.6 per cent average; and the United States with an average level of 4.9 per cent.
Which country in the industrial world has the worst average of unemployment? It is our own. The average rate of unemployment for that period in Canada, I am ashamed to say, was 5.4 per cent. That was up to 1974. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald)-who is in the chamber today-knows better than anyone else, the average since 1974 has become worse, not better.
This government has done virtually nothing. We raised this issue last fall at the opening of parliament and in special debates just before Christmas. Even after a month's recess at Christmas the government did not come back with a commitment to do something to provide jobs for the more than one million Canadians out of work. If we look at what they are doing now in terms of allocation of funds for direct job creation, compared with a few years ago when the level of unemployment was lower, we see they are even doing proportionately less than at that time. For the year 1971-72, when the unemployment level was 6.4 per cent, the government spent $603 million on direct job-creation programs. In 197677, when the unemployment rate had jumped to 7.1 per cent, the amount spent by this government on direct job-creation programs had dropped to $264 million. For 1977-78, the current fiscal year, with an unemployment average being
Unemployment
forecast for the year 1977 of between 7.5 per cent and 8 per cent, this government plans to spend only $243 million in direct job-creation programs.
Surely this is a scandal. It is something that a government with any sense of human priorities would not tolerate. A few years ago, when unemployment was significantly lower, they were spending almost three times the amount in job-creation programs. The government is an uncaring one, one that is motivated, in terms of people-oriented programs, only a few months before an election. It is a disgrace.
Having said these things about the government, I must say that I regard the official opposition, to understate it, with considerable skepticism as they now express their concern about unemployment. I simply cannot understand that party putting a motion before the House at this time which does not even call for a vote of non-confidence in the government. This at a time when there are over one million people out of work. In recent weeks and months that party has proposed changes to government programs that most seriously affect those from parts of Canada about which today they are allegedly expressing concern. I refer to the changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act which were first advocated by the financial spokeman for the Conservative party, who was in the chamber a few moments ago. These changes were also actively supported by the labour critic of the Conservative party of Canada.
Those two men, before the Liberal government of Canada brought forward this change in the unemployment insurance regulations, both inside and outside the House said that the basic entitlement period for a person to be eligible for unemployment insurance should be changed from the existing one of eight weeks to 12 weeks. It was the Conservatives who made that recommendation. It is the Conservatives who are now saying we should be concerned about the problems of Atlantic Canada and the province of Quebec.

doesn't matter whether he is in Ontario, Atlantic Canada or British Columbia. My party would not tolerate the kind of hypocrisy which has been indulged in by the Tories on this issue.

I want to put on record the number of Canadians in Atlantic Canada who will be directly affected by this Tory idea taken over by the Liberals. speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO GENERATE JOBS
speechtext:
I appreciate the consideration of my colleagues and I shall try not to abuse it. I was listing the revenue which would be lost to the provinces of Atlantic Canada, and Quebec, because of the changes in the unemployment insurance law as proposed by the Conservative party and accepted by the Liberal government. Nova Scotia would lose between $9 million and $11 million for the coming year, and New Brunswick between $19 million and $22 million. In the province of Quebec, about which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Clark) rightly said we should be particularly concerned at this point in our history, the loss will be between $93 million and $102 million. This money would be directly beneficial to the families suffering from unemployment. It would also have a good effect on the economy, because these people, if they got the money, would be spending it.
We have said that something has to be done about unemployment. We say it should have been done last fall, two weeks ago, last week. We shall be happy if the minister will act next week. Maybe he will be moved now that the figure of over one million Canadians unemployed has sunk into his mind with all

its human implications. We have called for direct tax cuts for people in the low and medium income brackets who will spend the money and stimulate the economy which at the present time is only operating at 85 per cent of capacity in the manufacturing centre.
We have called for the reactivation of government work programs which were put aside during the period of restraint, programs which would stimulate expansion at the municipal level across Canada. Third, we have called for a significant increase in home construction, low income housing, to meet both the need of job creation and the human need for decent accommodation. Finally, as a short-run measure, we have urged the government to take steps to provide new and extended insulation capacity in federal offices and residential buildings right across Canada. The government took up that suggestion more than a month ago and applied it to Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. We asked that there should be a national program in this area. This would not only create jobs; it would help toward the solution of an almost equally important question, the conservation of energy.
These, Mr. Speaker, are concrete steps which ought to be taken by a government which is truly concerned about the right of Canadians to work and the loss to our economy resulting from a million Canadians wanting to do something but being out of work. It is not enough, of course, for a government to deal simply with unemployment. It must simultaneously set up a mechanism to plan the national economy. This is what has been done in Sweden, in West Germany, in Norway and in Japan. A policy which deals with inflation for a time, moves on to deal with unemployment and then switches back again, is not good enough. We must plan the economy in a rational way so as to minimize, in a modern market economy, the amount of inflation while maximizing the number of jolts available for those who want them. That is the real issue.
Our party is committed to maintaining the capacity of our people to realize themselves as responsible citizens in their communities and among their families, and the most effective way in which they can do so is by finding jobs. It is time the government showed more sympathy with that objective.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words: "This House also urges that the government
(1)	immediately decrease personal income taxes for those in the lower and middle incomes to stimulate purchasing power and take up the current slack in the economy,
(2)	immediately reactivate all federal capital works projects and encourage the provinces and municipalities to follow suit, and at the same time, lift any restraint on shared funding of such projects,
(3) immediately expand-in consultation with the provinces-the capital budgets for low income and co-operative housing and land assembly,
(4)	immediately launch an assisted repair and renovation program of homes owned by pensioners, the disabled and low-income families, and
(5)	immediately launch a program-in co-operation with the provinces-of insulating or improving the level of insulation in all residential buildings-a program which would provide not only jobs but would also conserve energy."
February 10, 1977

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion today provides a useful opportunity, by way of preparation for the budget, to hear the views of the various groups within the House on possible measures of economic stimulus that might be taken, just as in recent weeks I have taken the occasion to discuss the approach of the executive of the Canadian Labour Congress, that of various groups across the country and, of course, most recently that of the provincial governments last week.
By way of introduction, I would just indicate that my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) will be participating in the debate and talking in particular about specific federal commitments for industrial expansion, and more specifically in the province of Quebec. My colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) will also be participating for the purpose of talking about his direct job-creation program.
Therefore, what I should like to do is to talk about some of the fiscal and monetary measures which have been effective within the last several months in particular in stimulating personal disposable income; to indicate that in many respects the measures which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Clark) and the leader of the New Democratic Party have put before the House are already incorporated in measures the government is taking; and also to make some comments relating to the very serious and important concern that exists about unemployment and the very serious concern we must have and continue to have respecting the level of inflation in Canada.
Firstly, I would review once more for the House the measures we have taken in the category of enriching personal disposable income. By a series of measures previously taken through legislative action in this parliament and effective as of January 1, 1977, there has been a transfer from the federal public sector of approximately $1,700 million, on an annual basis, to the incomes of individual Canadians. Indeed, adding to this particular transfer the equally automatic transfer that is effected by indexation of provincial tax in the nine provinces which participate in the tax-sharing agreements, there is approximately $2 billion worth of fiscal transfers, on an annual basis, which has gone to the incomes of Canadians. What this, therefore, means is that the various measures which have been taken in Canada will have some effect, indeed in percentage terms greater effect, on personal incomes of Canadians than the tax cut measures which President Carter has indicated it is his intention to put to the United States Congress.
Let me review these measures again in some detail. Firstly, the income tax indexation is well known to the House and I would only rehearse the figures involved. Canadians but for the indexing operation, would have had to pay, on an annual basis, in 1977 $950 million more than in fact they will now have to pay. Indeed, starting from the deductions effective as of January 1, 1977, those tax cuts are already going into the incomes of individual Canadians. As I have indicated, with the automatic indexing which is offered under the tax-sharing
Unemployment
arrangements with the provinces, a further approximately $300 million has been flowing into the incomes of Canadians in the nine participating provinces in addition to the amounts of reduced federal income tax.
In terms of specific groups in the community, many of whom are in the middle and lower income groups, there have been not just tax reductions but actual increases in transfer payments-an increase in the transfer payments to old age security recipients of $390 million, on an annual basis, and to the recipients of family allowance $160 million, also on an annual basis. In other words, the senior citizens of Canada and families with children are already receiving increased payments on a monthly basis over those they were receiving in December, 1976.
Further, the working people of Canada, people in the work force who are contributors to and participants in the unemployment insurance program, are as of January 1, 1977, paying less by way of contributions to the program than they were required to pay in the year 1976. This reduction in unemployment insurance contributions amounts, on an annual basis, to $250 million. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, that on the basis of these various measures which are offered under existing legislation there has been a return to individual taxpayers, on an annual basis, of close to $2 billion in terms either of transfer payments or obligations to pay tax which have been forgone.
But that is not all in terms of stimulative effect, Mr. Speaker. I have talked about the impact of fiscal policy and I think I should also draw to the attention of the House the fact that within the last three months, with three successive reductions in the bank rate, the Bank of Canada, in monetary policy terms, has also increased the personal disposable incomes of Canadians. If I may make reference to a statement that was made at the first ministers' meeting on February 1, 1977, it was said there:
We estimate that Canadian families, over time, stand to save about $1 billion a year in interest charges for each percentage point decline in interest rates. This saving breaks down into about $250 million on consumer loans and $750 million on mortgages. This, in itself, represents a substantial net addition to personal disposable incomes. There can be no doubt that it also strengthens consumer and business confidence.
That quotation is not of myself but of the provincial treasurer of Ontario, Hon. Darcy W. McKeough, who was talking about a $1 billion reduction for each point in the interest rate. Given the fact that the interest rate has gone down 1 !6 points, the reduction will be even more than that. Therefore, the combination of the reduction in income tax, the increase in transfer payments, and the reduction in the bank rate and, therefore, in interest rates that are payable by Canadians, has increased personal disposable income by more than $3 billion. These are measures which have been effective within the last two or three months. So when hon. gentlemen talk about further measures to stimulate personal disposable income, they are obviously ignoring the fact that those measures are already operative within the economy, that individual Canadians are already being spared additional tax or interest payments

which, but for these measures supported by this government, Canadians would have had to pay.
If I may go to some of the remarks made so far, may I first comment on the speech of the leader of the opposition and then that of the leader of the New Democratic Party. In his remarks the leader of the opposition made reference to job-creation rates. I think I would have to emphasize that one has to be concerned at the current level of unemployment in Canada, and one has to guard, as well, against any undue optimism when presented with the figures for January, 1977. But there are some elements which could have a positive potential from the standpoint of the work force. I refer, for example, to the fact that since December, 1976, there were
69,000	created jobs among that group within the age bracket 15 to 24, which is one of the groups which has been most severely hit by increased unemployment since August, 1976.
In other words, for the first time since that year the figure respecting the younger members of the work force has turned around and shows an increase in the month of January. In addition to that, smaller increases occurred in the number of men and women over that particular age, making for an increase of 79,000 jobs in Canada since December, 1976.
The hon. gentleman made reference to the government's having ignored Quebec in regard to particular measures, and my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, who is here with us for this debate, will have a specific opportunity to give, chapter and verse, the measures which have been taken under his direction to provide an active and more competitive economy for that particular province.
I followed with interest-because it was important to follow the suggestions of the leader of the opposition-some of the measures that he would have included if the presenting of a budget had been within his responsibilities. I find again, as I have already said in my general statements, that there is a substantial measure of agreement between the hon. gentleman and myself. Indeed, to a very great degree the points which he enunciated are ones which are now effective or operating favourably in the economy. If I understood him correctly, he would, if he had responsibility, have committed himself to no increase in government expenditures. That has been the policy of this government.

speechtext: That is right.

That has been the policy since the statement of October, 1975, and, indeed, will continue to be one of the elements which guides us in our continued concern about the impact of inflation in Canada. The hon. gentleman said that he would have preferred stimulating consumer demand, he having said at another point that the Carter administration has stimulated consumer demand by allowing increased personal disposable income. Therefore, why should not the same thing be done in Canada? Of course, I just dealt with that, Mr. Speaker, by pointing out measures which will

provide about $3 billion on an annual basis. They are now in place and in operation.
Let me say a word about housing. I make this comment both to the Leader of the Opposition and to the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). It is interesting to note that despite all the rhetoric one hears about the housing policies espoused by this government, particularly those set forth to this House by my colleague who is now Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) but who was then minister of state for urban affairs, this government created on an annual basis in 1976 the highest rate of housing unit construction which we have known in Canada. The figure as at the close of the year was 279,000 units. That is the highest level of housing starts which we have achieved in Canadian history.

speechtext: Yes, but the population is higher, too.

speechtext:
It is well above the level stipulated by the government when it said it would need to create one million new housing units in the next four years. The rate is well above the annual rate necessary to achieve that. It is interesting to note, in connection with the building of those
279.000	housing units across Canada, that the government of Canada, through various programs introduced by my colleague, has been responsible for assisting in the creation of
120.000	of those additional housing units, particularly for those at the lower end of the income scale. I had occasion to refer to this fact in recent days during the course of debate when dealing with projects such as the Dundas-Sherbourne project in my constituency which will provide housing for low-income Canadians at the bottom of the income scale. As well, the government has assisted many others at the middle range of the scale, through the Assisted Home Ownership Program, in being able to finance a home. In general terms, the government has provided substantial assistance and has made a substantial contribution to the achievement of the record figure mentioned. Indeed, although the current rate of housing starts observed in January, 1977, has fallen off the dramatic rate obtained in 1976, the rate has not fallen off severely. I notice that the rate for 1977 is projected at 268,400 houses, which still represents a substantial contribution and is still ahead of the target which the minister set forth in his statement one year ago.
I now come to regional development incentives. I think we shall need to study what the leader of the opposition said in this respect.

speechtext: That program is a farce.

We shall need to see to what extent his proposals vary from the substantial panoply of measures which the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) now has in operation particularly in Quebec and Atlantic Canada. I noted one interesting innovation contained in the remarks of the leader of the opposition-his suggestion that particular assistance should be given to research and development projects of corporations. I shall take careful note
February 10, 1977

of the hon. gentleman's words in this regard in the course of the preparation of my budget.
I now turn to the leader of the NDP. He began by saying, as he has so often in the past, that we have ignored job creation in Canada. My colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, will in an effective way be able to deal with programs which he has put in place for the purpose of direct job creation. The hon. gentleman raised an interesting point and suggested that because the rate of growth of the Canadian economy is down, some Canadians are not making the level of income they might otherwise expect and other Canadians are therefore paying a greater level of taxes. That is not correct. Indeed, as I have already said, the level of taxation is down as a result both of the tax measure which we hope will soon be enacted and as a result of indexing.
Therefore, there has been no increase in the impact of taxation upon Canadians. On the contrary, there has been a reduction. Of course, the federal government by assuming a deficit has for this period of time been prepared to pick up the difference in order to avoid imposing an additional burden.
As I have pointed out already, the direct tax cuts are in effect. Approximately 120,000 housing units have been provided for those who are largely in the low and middle income brackets. These measures have already been put into effect.
Let me make an observation about the amendment which has been moved. The hon. gentleman opposite talked about unemployment at present, but he is not concerned about present unemployment when the building season starts or when planning can be completed and major projects undertaken later this year and in 1978. In that sense it is difficult to follow his reasoning when he suggests there should be reactivation of federal capital works projects and that provinces and municipalities should be encouraged to follow suit. For reasons which I have indicated many times previously, we think there must be restraint on public expenditures in Canada in order to provide an opportunity and room for expansion in private expenditures. It is clear that legislation enacted to provide for capital works projects would not for months and months produce any major new jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with calmness and courtesy to the leader of the NDP. Perhaps his eager colleagues might show me the same courtesy. Whether or not any capital projects are now brought forward, it is fair to observe that any such projects would not assist substantially this current winter in dealing with present levels of unemployment.
Before I conclude my remarks, let me say that I have given an indication to the House of the increase in personal disposable income which has resulted from the fiscal and monetary
Unemployment
policies espoused by this government. I have indicated the direct expenditures which the government has made in fields such as housing and direct employment creation. In a few minutes the House will hear from my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, to the same effect.
In closing, I wish to bring to the attention of the House a matter of fundamental concern since it is important to look at the economy in a balanced way. We do not think we can look on the economy with one eye, as the hon. gentleman opposite did. One of the factors which distinguished the speeches of both hon. gentlemen who preceded me was that they, apparently, are happy with the 6 per cent rate of inflation in Canada. They were not concerned enough about the inflationary challenge which Canada faces at present. They showed no evidence of concern with respect to what a continuation of inflation at the present rate, or even several points below the present rate, would do to Canada's economic competitive position in the long run.
When debating the economy of our country, it is fundamental to understand that we cannot afford "one issue politicians", politicians who talk one day about inflation, the next day about unemployment. We need to take a balanced look at the economic problems we face and, at the same time, try to bring forward measures which will deal with unemployment in particular sectors of the economy such as younger age groups. At the same time, we need to deal with structural problems which are evident in certain regions. But we have to do so within a framework which makes certain that the success we have gained until now in reducing the double-digit rate of inflation to below 6 per cent is not only a gain that can be held but one that can be added to by even further reduction, because in the long run the problem of inflation is also the problem of unemployment.
If Canada continues to run a level of inflation above that of our industrial competitors, if we continue to have a level of industrial costs and a level of industrial wages in particular that runs substantially above those in the countries against which we compete in foreign markets and which compete against us in our own markets, then we will not only be concerned about the impact of inflationary increases on our personal lives but people will be concerned about losing their jobs, for the loss of competitiveness by the Canadian industry will mean, in the long run, a far greater challenge to the job picture in Canada than any of the temporary changes in the economic cycle which we have known up to this time.
I would like to say one more thing in closing, I think the leader of the opposition employed some admirable rhetoric in talking about our country. At the start he spoke about the growth potential and the promise and possibility of Canada. I agree with those two terms. I think we do have an enormous growth potential, and there is enormous promise and possibility in Canada. But one thing we have to remember, all of us from political leaders through to the working man on the assembly line, is that while we have enjoyed a very high

Unless we are effective in restraining the rate of inflation in Canada, we are not only not going to be able to compete abroad but we will have difficulty sustaining the position of our manufacturing industry in our own markets. It is for this reason that 1 find many of the suggestions made by the hon. gentleman not to have been a constructive approach to the very serious economic problems which we have. But I would have to say, in all fairness, that one of the points made by the leader of the opposition was indeed a constructive suggestion, and several of those made by the leader of the NDP were in the same vein. I will consider those as I will be considering the suggestions and observations of many members of the House and many people throughout Canada in preparation for the budget which I hope to be presenting to this House within a matter of some months.
Just before I conclude-I see the leader of the opposition is back in the House after being out of it-I would like to say that I find myself in the same difficulty in which he found himself. Because of the shortness of notice, I was not able to move all my appointments, and I will not be able to remain in the chamber for all the speeches. I hope hon. members will not regard this as a discourtesy, and 1 apologize to them in advance.
