speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to take part in this debate. First 1 should like to thank the author of the motion and those who chose this opposition day to raise a matter so much discussed throughout the country. We know that when speaking about unemployment, there are huge difficulties involved. I really appreciate that the province I am living in was specifically mentioned together with Atlantic Canada which faces even more serious difficulties.
Mr. Speaker, I too listened to the speeches like the other members of the House. I heard the answers by the minister a few moments ago who was pointing out the effort his government had made, the expenditures his government had incurred, the decisions his government had taken recently. Of course the government has to make some decisions. What is unfortunate is that those decisions are often long overdue. The government takes decisions every day because it has to and it seems to me that the government was not able to do anything to foresee the difficulties and hardships that Canadians have been facing in recent years.
After listening to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) just said it seems that the situation is not so bad in this country. The government acted with enlightened moderation, and we just have to go out of this House to see the difficulties and the misery that we are now facing and not only in Quebec, but in several provinces of the country. I think that the question is very relevant and that it is important to recall certain things to hon. members.
I Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).]
I remember very well that in 1968, for example, when I came in this House as a new member, we were told that unemployment would be reduced. At that time, there were approximately 170,000 unemployed. The government had this very important goal which was included in its principle of a just society; it wanted to fight unemployment. There were
170,000	unemployed. Then, from that figure, we passed to 200,000, 300,000, 400,000, 500,000 and then came the inflation factor. I remember that the Prime Minister stated publicly: "You know, there are 500,000 unemployed and inflation is starting to eat up everyone's wallet. You will have to get used to unemployment." So, with about 500,000 unemployed, the government tried to have Canadians admit that unemployment was not only temporary, but that it would remain and that we had to take steps not to fight it but to maintain it. And that we had to create unemployment to fight inflation. Finally, Mr. Speaker, we have both, inflation and unemployment. I still hear the minister saying today; Despite all of this the situation is not too bad, the government has a sound administration.
There are many government members in this House who are very well aware of the difficulties facing Quebeckers. Of course, one would be tempted to accuse the provincial government, and not only the one in power since November 15. The difficulties the premier of Quebec had since 1966 with this government are well known and we recall that over the years the federal government has given more than one negative answer to recommendations made by Mr. Bourassa's members of cabinet. We all remember that but of course we will not talk too much about it today. Nevertheless, unemployment is in a precarious state in Quebec.
Those were this government's objectives and commitments. And if one dares accuse the government for failing to take action, for lack of vision, then we have no solutions. In addition, it seems that someone is always trying to make us believe that the government has done everything. If the government has really done everything, Mr. Speaker-I had counted 500,000 unemployed, but today, in 1977, the number has reached 800,000 and according to some very conservative economists, in 1978 we will break the one million barrier, as it were-well if that was the Prime Minister's objective, to get used to unemployment, 1 do not think Canadians are willing to pay for and support a million unemployed in the country.
So, Mr. Speaker, the only patent result of this government's administration in the last ten years is a complete failure as regards the fight against unemployment and inflation, I am led to believe that it was easier for the government to create unemployment than to create jobs. I think we will agree on that. There was also some talk about economic investments that would create jobs. We will be reminded of course of the extraordinary expenditures made by the Regional Economic Expansion Department to create new industries.
To what extent, for instance, has the government cared for the preservation and protection of our Canadian industries? Every day some of them close and many are expected to close
February 10, 1977

in the future. It seems that the government has yet to find the solutions that will help protect our Canadian industry first.
Of course the government is going to talk about its free trade policy. We must open our doors to friendly countries, but little effort has been made to protect our industry in Canada. Should I recall the dramatic situation in the textile industry and hon. members from Quebec who are here know this. The situation in this industry has deteriorated. Of course we had to accept foreign products but I do not think we were seriously concerned about the future of the textile industry, particularly in Quebec where it employs thousands of workers, and in high unemployment areas. This situation results from the lack of courage, the lack of audaciousness, the lack of initiative of a government towards a particular industry. Quebecers know what price they have to pay for it, when we consider that in the manufacturing sector one worker out of four is in the textile industry.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) made a statement recently; many people are concerned but he made a statement after God knows how many other ministers had let this industry fend for itself. This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) announced some economic injections or some cost-sharing programs, but the harm is done.
Flow would it be possible to give a new direction to this industry, to ensure the contribution our industries and Canadian workers are entitled to? How many years will it take for Canada to recover a market which was once controlled by a Canadian industry. Therefore I suggest once again that one can blame it on the weakness, the lack of leadership, of foresight or courage on the part of the government in its relations with importing countries.
A few days ago I was informed about the catastrophic situation in which the footwear industry finds itselfs. Questions are in the air, we are being asked: what are your solutions? We should see that industries be reoriented and stabilized as soon as possible. Some of them have closed their doors; the structure is still there, ready to receive workers and to manufacture something. No question of it and in the footwear industry the same policy applies. The policy was one of no intervention but our footwear industries have also difficulties, even in Quebec, and I am talking about federal decisions. Talk about public powers! That means important loss of jobs for the province of Quebec. But we will come back on that point later.
The government will compensate with fantastic amounts of money spent for social programs. There has been a good deal of leadership in that field. With social programs we are going to keep one million unemployed and we are going to increase pensions of every description but we are going to get people used to it and corrupt a whole generation with unemployment! A whole generation will get used to living on unemployment benefits and we are going to deny older people the right to retire at 60 if they wish to do so. We never said that old people should be compelled to retire at the age of 60, but I wonder why should the government not consider that people aged 60 and concerned about their physical condition might find it
Unemployment
logical and rewarding to ask for a well deserved rest and a well deserved pension, and leave room for the thousands of unemployed young people we have in this country. From the point of view of productivity, it is far from being outstanding. The possibility of creating an optional retirement pension has been mentioned to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I do not mean anything compulsory. Thousands of people between 60 and 65 might feel ready for a little rest after having served their country and worked in industry during 40 years. But, no, it would be too expensive. Maybe the government thinks it is a better idea to maintain almost one million unemployed.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, it seems easier for this government to find money or new ways to maintain thousands of people without work than to create job opportunities. Should I remind hon. members that agriculture was far from being a success in 1976. I remember that some of our friends from Quebec on the other side were far from being happy with the government policy. I even remember hearing the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) confess publicly, barely three weeks ago on television, on a Sunday night, that his government has made a colossal error with regard to its dairy policy. He did not say so in the House, but he did in answer to questions put to him that night. I have not heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) support the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, but I do agree with the hon. member for Papineau when he says that colossal errors were made with regard to the dairy policy.
We know what that cost Quebec last year, and that Ontario producers paid through the nose, as a consequence. But once again, credits will be voted for social measures and we will be expected to applaud the government. That is why we feel the government has failed in its responsibilities, because it did not have the foresight, the courage and, above all, the initiative to plan employment, I should say to protect and keep what jobs there are in Canada. So, what was done to protect and encourage Canadian industries is not too bright. This opposition day gives us the opportunity of reminding the government that we are asking it to provide money for creating new jobs, but the most basic decency demands that we should first of all save our industries and protect those jobs, especially when we know that Canadian consumption can use up Canadian production.
As for housing, a small S500 program was provided to attract buyers and promote expansion in that field. It did not last long and, when we are faced with increased unemployment and huge difficulties, they take away the $500. Nowadays it would probably cost $1,000 to put the housing industry back on its feet again.
The minister mentioned earlier an increase granted last year to that effect for the number of units but failed to mention at what cost. And to think that today the average worker will commit himself for 30 years and pay in interest IV2 times the real value of his house! But they do not talk much about that.

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
The important thing for the government and producers is that policies have been set up with regards to loans and loan granting has been made easier. It posed no problem. Pay back when you can!
In agriculture, the same thing goes for milk producers. The government compelled farmers and milk producers to borrow, that no one can deny. Whenever someone wanted to borrow $30,000 from a farm loans office to upgrade his operations, the government would say: You cannot go wrong, you are going into the milk industry, you will have the good life, your children will follow. That is why you do not need $30,000 but $60,000. You do not want to buy 30 cows, you want 50.
Everything is settled and for a long time. But after only one year, the farmer had to give up a certain number of cows. I am not going to rehash the same story but the minister is looking at me and I am certain that people in his own riding have told him the same story. It is not the case only in my part of the country, it is the same everywhere. As a matter of fact, I remember that some Liberal members who sat on the Committee on Agriculture last year were not happy about this policy.
We now blame the government for not having had the necessary foresight, for having badly oriented certain groups of producers and also for having given thousands of Canadians illusions about their position and for not having been able to protect them at that level. I now would like to talk about the cuts in research budgets. In the long term, Mr. Speaker, we know how costly this can be for Canada. Experts tell us so, and I am not the one who invented this, I would not be able to do so. I have read some material like everyone else. Some people want to cut expenditures in research. Once again we shall let foreign countries make the inventions and we shall once again depend on these countries to sell them to us at the prices that they will choose. But it is not a part of government policy to provide, maintain and emphasize research to constantly protect Canadian industry, for Canadians and by Canadians. I think this would be more logical. But no, cuts must be made! There is growing concern about this and university specialists tell us about this, not only to us, members of the opposition, but to all members of parliament, and the government is surely aware of it.
Earlier the minister explained the efforts that he is making. Mr. Speaker, we have to be glad about this opposition day on unemployment and take the opportunity to repeat certain things as I am doing. As a Quebecker, I deplore the inertia that the federal government has shown for too long and its lack of foresight, which has been very costly and which has placed the province of Quebec in a difficult situation because of extremely high unemployment rates.
I was looking at unemployment levels in various areas. I know that certain members on the other side must be terribly concerned when, for instance, the rates are up to 19 per cent in northern Quebec. In some places, they are up to 11 per cent and 13 per cent. The situation is bad in the Gaspe Peninsula when the unemployment rate has reached 22 per cent. We would be happy to listen to the Minister of Finance say that

the government has made tremendous efforts and that we should be satisfied with these efforts.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time has expired and I hope that this day will have been beneficial by urging the government to reflect about what has been said in the House today. I would like to repeat that in Quebec, we are waiting for the government to take specific stands. I assume that Quebeckers opposite will take this opportunity to remind their government they have failed miserably to remedy the unemployment situation for lack of a policy.

Minister said a few days ago in this House-as long as there is one Canadian in this country who wants to work and cannot find a job we will not be satisfied. We work from that principle. What we want to do is try to improve the situation considering the circumstances in which we find ourselves.
We have problems, I admit, but if hon. members opposite want to give us credit for it, which 1 doubt, I will say that in the last three years while the United States of America, the most powerful western country in existence, was for 27 months in a period of recession we, in Canada, managed to go through a period that was not one of recession. We did not have a period of great economic growth but we went through a period in which we did not go below the zero line as was the case for the Americans during 27 consecutive months. We encountered certain difficulties but of all countries of the western world in the last three years we were probably one of those which were the most successful. In spite of that I must admit we had problems and that we still have problems. But the problems we face in Canada are probably not more difficult to solve and not more serious than those of other countries.
I understand the hon. member, and I agree with him when he says that it is not good that workers who want to work should not find jobs. However, I believe that we managed in Canada in the last 15 years to give ourselves a social structure that allowed us to reduce to a certain extent the ill effects of unemployment. Today we can be proud of the fact that generally speaking in our society there is suffering but nobody is starving or freezing. There are always a few individuals who for particular reasons are in that predicament. But this government's program vis-a-vis the social needs of the people of this country is probably the best in existence to the point where today many Canadians claim that the fact that we have such a generous unemployment insurance plan has become for certain people an escape door to avoid their responsibilities vis-a-vis work.
1 would not want to waste my time in this large debate. I would rather simply concentrate on what we have done in recent months to provide specific help for certain industries in difficulty, particularly in answer to the motion by the leader of the opposition whom we saw reappear in the House. He does not come here often. We are quite happy to see him when he shows up, and see him today raise the problem of Quebec and the Maritime provinces.

Mr. Speaker, we can all relax. I wish the 29,000 who are officially unemployed in Newfoundland had been watching the minister this afternoon. If they could have watched him speaking they would have understood us when we talk about an arrogant government. He tells us the government has done all that is possible to deal with the situation. If that is his admission, let him get out of office, because if the result of doing everything that is possible is to limit the unemployment figure to 800,000, and 29,000 in Newfoundland, to say nothing of the present figure in Quebec, he should get out of office.
The hon. gentleman is scooting quickly out of the chamber now, so we can relax. The hon. gentleman had the gall to mention, as a feather in his cap, the loan he is making for five ships to be built in Marystown. Newfoundland had to beg on bended knees to get the hon. gentleman even to consider that and to get the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) to push for it. Then they tried to screw Newfoundland into having to put their credit on the line as well, and he claimed that to his credit. I say it is a shame that he did not agree to it long ago. Originally there were ten ships, not just five. So don't regard Marystown, Newfoundland, as any great employment creation job done by the minister in the last few months.
I could not believe my ears when I heard the minister say that there was no danger of his losing his seat. By golly, Mr. Speaker, I hope that the electorate in his constituency will hear about that. If a minister of the government or if any member of the House thinks that this wonderful, tremendous minister, who is doing such a job of creating so much work and who is so perfect, is not in danger of losing his seat, let me tell them that his seat will be in jeopardy at the next election.
This is a government which has the gall to call a program the Canada Works program. They should be calling it the "Canada does not work program", not the Canada Works program. To create work is why we need this wonderful program. They are giving Canada the works; that is their

program. In view of the smug and arrogant speech made in this House today on unemployment, which is at its highest ever in the land, and particularly high in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, it is not any wonder that this government is in such disfavour and has but one straw to grasp, Quebec, which they are going to use for all they are worth. However, they are going there anyway as soon as the electorate gets the chance to put them out.
I only have 20 minutes, Mr. Speaker, so let me come to the motion, which reads;
That this House denounces the government's failure to generate jobs in Canada, particularly in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, and urges immediate and resolute action, including the early presentation of a budget.
I do not need to spend much time on how bad the situation is in Newfoundland because that is well known. In my maiden speech in this House I spoke on this exact subject, I think on November 15. Nothing has happened since then except that the situation has become worse. In Newfoundland the actual unemployment figure is 17.1 per cent; that is the Statistics Canada figure. This amounts to 29,000 unemployed. To those we must add 8,000 or 9,000 able-bodied on relief, and all of those who are not looking for work because they know they cannot find it. Then we must add the low participation rate, which is about 15 per cent below the national average, and several other factors I mentioned which indicate that the real unemployment rate in Newfoundland is at least 25 per cent to 30 per cent. And the hon. gentleman opposite says the government is doing all it can! Well, I will tell him about a few things it is not doing before I sit down.
The government is taking a cruel and inhuman attitude in ignoring regional differences in Canada. There are a number of other factors which show what the situation is in Atlantic Canada. I looked last night at the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program which is an official document of the government's advisory council. In 1974, when the situation was not as bad as it is now, the Atlantic provinces had 8 per cent of the labour force, but 16.8 per cent of the beneficiaries of unemployment insurance. Quebec had 27.1 per cent of the labour force and 36.4 per cent of the beneficiaries. When you look at how long the claims went on for, Atlantic Canada averaged 22.5 weeks in 1973 and the prairies averaged 15.4 weeks. In 1974 the Atlantic provinces averaged 21.8 weeks and the prairies 12.3 weeks. The claim rate in the Atlantic provinces was 63 per cent above the national average, and the cost ratio was 2.2 times the average. In Newfoundland, in 1973, we had 4 per cent of total benefits and only 2 per cent of the population. The situation in 1976 was much worse, and it will be the same in 1977.
What is the government's solution? It is to bring a bill before this House to change the eligibility requirements from eight weeks to 12 weeks, which has removed 16,500 people from eligibility in Newfoundland and will take $28 million out of the economy of Newfoundland in 1977 and 1978. The Progressive Conservative party will be moving an amendment, which the minister said the other day-I hope he changes his mind-the government will not accept, to the effect that in
February 10, 1977

areas of high unemployment, in areas considerably higher than the national average, the eligibility period should remain at eight weeks in recognition of their higher unemployment rate, the fact that the people in the area cannot get jobs, as well as other factors that I mentioned earlier. It is the same recognition as that given in the provision that permits a person to have benefits for a longer period, depending on the region in which he lives. The principle is the same.
We agreed to the 12-week measure in areas where unemployment has not been allowed by the government to become the tragedy which it is in the Atlantic provinces. If the hon. gentleman for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was conducting a filibuster the other day, it will be nothing compared with the filibuster that I intend to attempt to conduct if hon. gentlemen opposite do not accept some reasonable amendment such as this.
I have outlined the problem. What is the solution? There has been no solution offered so far. There has been a retrograde amendment to the unemployment insurance legislation that we hope to correct. Although the Canadian economy is bad and the forecast for this year is not good-I will not go into all the details-in Newfoundland we have not had a 1 per cent improvement in the gross provincial product; it was not 1 per cent better in 1975 or 1976, and it is forecast to be no better in 1977.
The level of construction is very low, unemployment is very high. Prospects for this year are very poor. We need to have a budget brought down which will stimulate the Canadian economy, will provide encouragement for investment and help regional economies. We need tax cuts to stimulate spending. We are also going to need increased government spending in certain areas where there is very high unemployment, such as Newfoundland, the Atlantic provinces and Quebec, on capital projects and on general government services so as to tackle the problem of high unemployment. Yes, there has to be some restraint of government expenditure, but more has to be spent in areas of this country which are a living scandal, such as Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces with their unemployment rates.
The provincial governments of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and P.E.l. cannot solve this problem. I cannot say about Quebec. They think they are miracle workers, and perhaps they can, so we will wait and see. But I know that in the four Atlantic provinces the provincial governments do not have the financial capacity or borrowing power to solve the problem. They do not control the Bank of Canada. They do not print the currency. They do not control the money supply. Their hands are tied. Newfoundland has been borrowing a couple of hundred million a year for the last four or five years, and they cannot borrow any more. They are doing everything they can. They have now introduced a little program worth $2 million for job-creation purposes and it is all that anyone can expect of them.
It is the federal government that has to help in this situation. It is the federal government that has the fiscal capacity and flexibility to help, and the Newfoundland government has

asked the federal government to help. When I was a minister of that government in December of 1975 and all during 1976, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was our representative in the cabinet, and he has been forgetting Newfoundland. He is turning his back on Newfoundland. What help has he pushed through to help Newfoundland in its extreme need? Nothing except Canada Works.

The embarrassment is that which the opposition parties have suffered in the last few votes we have had when they have been unable to muster more than 60 or 65 members for a vote. I am not surprised, therefore, that they have not been able to get a sufficient number of members to vote on this non-issue.
There is no doubt that the Canadian economy now faces and has faced, particularly since 1975, serious economic problems including, in particular, the problem of unemployment, and nobody is hiding that under the rug. Back in October we indicated our concern, we looked at reports that were coming in, and we initiated measures that were going to be taken.
If we are to understand these problems and deal with them effectively we must see them in perspective and not through some political rhetoric such as we have had here this afternoon from the hon. member for St. John's West.
We must recognize that we have not been alone in facing these problems; we must also remember that over the longer period of the 1960's and early 1970's the performance of the

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
Canadian economy was exceptionally strong. During this period the growth rate of the economy was of the order of 5 per cent. The growth in employment was of the order of 3 per cent. Even during this healthy period there were specific times of difficulty as, for example, in 1967 and 1970-71. This is the typical pattern of all free economies, that is, alternative periods of rapid and slow growth.
The unique feature of the Canadian economy during this period was the rapid growth in the labour force of 3 per cent to 4 per cent, particularly arising out of the dramatic influx of youths and women into the labour market; in fact, during the period, and except for a few recent months, we experienced the highest growth rate in the labour force of any western industrialized country.
I read an article by Mr. MacGillivray, whose research is usually well documented, and I was surprised that he saw fit to pick one particular time frame when he said Canada's labour force was not the fastest growing in the western industrialized world. I wonder why he felt it necessary to pinpoint that area. Nevertherless, the growth of the economy during this period was sufficient to provide the required additional jobs to keep unemployment rates relatively low for the period as a whole.
The following are the specific problems of unemployment put in this perspective. We are still faced with a rapid growth in the labour force. But, at the same time, we are faced with relatively slow economic growth rates. We are not alone in facing this problem. For us, however, it is worse than for many other countries because of the openness and vulnerability of the Canadian economy to the changing economic situation of our major trading partners, particularly the United States. Our ability to devise satisfactory remedies for our problems, we must remember, has been severely constrained since we have found ourselves in the grip of serious inflationary forces.
Given this perspective, what is the government's response? Faced with these problems and constraints on action, the government has adopted selective measures to help prevent and alleviate the serious problem of unemployment. Briefly, the government's employment strategy includes the following: a doubling of the LIP funds for the current winter period to $200 million; the launching of a year-round Canada Works program involving the expenditure in 1977-78 of some $200 million on direct job-creation; and the strengthening of rehabilitative or preventative measures, for example, through training involving annual expenditures close to $600 million.
I think the government, recognizing the problem, has pinpointed the areas where, given the restraints we have, and given the fact that we do not want to be inflationary, help must be given, and we have pumped millions of dollars into these areas, notwithstanding the sloughing off which the hon. member for St. John's West thought we should do with millions of dollars. Under LIP we have pumped $17 million into the island of Newfoundland alone.
The selective measures, particularly direct job-creation projects, in which 120,000 individuals will participate in 197778, have two critically important advantages. First, they rank amongst the best employment measures in terms of cost per

job created and in terms of generating employment quickly. Indeed, they have been a model on which other countries have based their own job-creation programs.
Second, the government's job-creation programs can be, and are, targeted to groups and communities most seriously affected by the problems of unemployment. For example, we have special programs for youths and the disadvantaged. We have also allocated the largest proportion of job-creation funds to the provinces east of the Ottawa river which are suffering acute unemployment problems. We are also allocating a large proportion of job-creation funds to meet the more severe problems of unemployment during the winter season.
We must not lose sight of the fact that the Unemployment Insurance program is a major bulwark against the problem of income deficiency arising out of unemployment. By supporting the level of individual incomes, it helps in a significant way to maintain the over-all level of demand within the economy. This in turn helps to sustain a higher level of employment.
The combined expenditures of unemployment insurance and the departmental appropriations will involve the expenditure in 1977-78 of some $4.5 billion to help alleviate or prevent unemployment in Canada. We have embarked on this with a spirit of innovation. We have been sensitive to the changing nature of unemployment, the labour market, and the economy, as well as the limitations of traditional approaches.
I note that the hon. member who spoke before me seems to be satisfied to stay with the status quo, to keep to the eight weeks and not to use the money. He seems to be saying-and that concerns me-that we should now go to selective areas in the country and move back to the eight week program. We are using that money as a lever to get more money. If the hon. member would look at the individual figures, and particularly those for Newfoundland, he would see that from the small amount of money that is coming from the unemployment insurance program we will be in a position to pump three, four and five times that much money into the economy of Newfoundland, given the leverage I have indicated.
We are approaching these changing problems in a spirit of innovation. Specifically, we have included in Bill C-27 provision for the developmental uses of the unemployment insurance funds so that claimants will have a variety of productive program alternatives while they are receiving their benefits. These include participation in training programs, job-creation projects, and work sharing arrangements. The latter two, which will be launched on a pilot project basis, could lay the ground work for new and more successful approaches to deal with problems of unemployment in the future. Canada can be proud of its innovative nature in dealing with the specific problem.
Criticism of the measures of unemployment causes me no little concern. Recent comments made by some members of parliament have unfortunately confused the discussion of the scope and nature of unemployment problems. Various measures of unemployment published by Statistics Canada inevita-
February 10, 1977

bly have their limitations, and these are well recognized by Statistics Canada itself. They are, however, incomparably more reliable as indicators of the scope and nature of unemployment and changing trends than the statistics concocted, interpreted and misinterpreted by some. A particular case in point is the recent assertion made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) to the effect that the unemployment rate for 1976 was really closer to 11 per cent than the 7 per cent reported.
Specifically, the hon. member contends that during that year some 455,000 people who were laid off or who had lost their jobs should have been counted among the unemployed rather than among the non-labour force, as they were in fact counted in the labour force survey. He maintains that these people are "discouraged workers" or "the hidden unemployed".
The hon. member has no factual basis for making this assertion. In the first place, the 455,000 people to whom he refers were laid off or lost their jobs at any time within the previous five years. Moreover, there is no indication whether on termination of their jobs any of these people searched for work or even had an interest in continuing to work. But what we do know is that they were not looking for work at the time the labour force survey was conducted.
The hon. member also ignores the fact that this category includes people whose jobs ended due to seasonal factors, such as the end of the fishing, logging, trapping, farming or tourist season. We know that many of these people are interested only in that type of seasonal work.
Many studies of the problems of "discouraged workers" have concluded that while statistics in this group should be gathered, the people who comprise it should not be counted as unemployed. Indeed, statistical agencies throughout the world have found that a definition of unemployment incorporating a measure of an individual's desire to find work is far too subjective and ambiguous to permit the production of objective, meaningful and consistent data.
However, we recognize the limitations, and what is our approach? Our approach to the question of the limitations of using Statistics Canada figures as sole indicators of unemployment is much more equitable, objective and defensible. In particular, in the formula for allocating funds in the first phase of the Canada Works program we have included statistics on unemployment insurance beneficiaries. Specifically, we have used such beneficiary statistics in the case of those provinces where the number of beneficiaries exceeds the number of labour force survey unemployed.
This approach, on an objective basis, helps to compensate for certain limitations in the labour force survey definition of unemployment. For example, unemployment insurance beneficiary statistics include those who are virtually unemployed but have earnings from part-time employment. Such individuals may be counted as beneficiaries, but they are excluded from the labour force survey unemployed.
Unemployment
Therefore, in the provinces east of the Ottawa river, the number of unemployment insurance beneficiaries is higher than the labour force survey unemployed. Selecting the higher measure results in the allocation of a large proportion of Canada Works funds to provinces east of the Ottawa River, where it is recognized that the problem of unemployment is more serious. In the case of Newfoundland this involves an increase of some 50 per cent in the measure of unemployment, to give some degree of equity to these particular statistics.
In the case of the provinces west of the Ottawa River, it is to their advantage to use the labour force survey unemployed, which is higher than the number of unemployment insurance beneficiaries. This is attributable in part to the number of people who are unemployed but do not qualify for unemployment insurance benefits.
The use of unemployment insurance beneficiary data in connection with the labour force survey thus achieves a balance which is not possible through the use of other sources of data alone.
None of us has the final solutions to the complex problems of unemployment. While our own employment and insurance programs are among the most advanced of any country in the world, we recognize that still more imaginative and concerted efforts are required. With this goal in mind, the government has undertaken a systematic review of the current unemployment situation and is reassessing programs and mixes of programs which are likely to be most effective in coming to grips with the problems of the next two years. At the same time we are carrying out an in-depth examination of the longer term aspects of employment and unemployment, so that we will be prepared to meet the problems of the next decade.
What is called for is a broad strategy which examines the widest possible variety of programs and approaches, ranging from the stimulation of the private sector to direct job-creation programs, where appropriate, and supplemented by income maintenance, where necessary. This strategy also involves a continuing search for innovative measures tailored to the ever changing dynamics of our society and economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a sad state of affairs for parliament and, therefore, for Canadians as a whole, that

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
while unemployment, according to the latest figures from Statistics Canada, is at the highest level since the formation of that department, that it is left to the official opposition to introduce a motion dealing with this serious subject matter rather than depending on the government to act.
It is not something that has developed overnight and caught the government unaware or ill-prepared with which to cope. As we all know, the unemployment figures have been creeping up steadily over the past decade of this Liberal administration's reign until they have reached this incredible level where nearly one million Canadians now find themselves without a job. Meantime, the government sits placidly by, working on the introduction of bills such as an Act to amend the Historic Sites and Monuments Act, or introduces for debate, after a one month Christmas recess, a bill to televise the proceedings of this House, a move that would surely bring about the deterioration of this Chamber into a three-ring circus. These are examples of the government's sense of priorities.
We cannot even blame it on international conditions because other western industrialized nations such as Japan and West Germany have virtually full employment, while at the same time we see the United States unemployment figures steadily decreasing, a fact based on that nation's own priorities and action.
Throughout this debate many reasons were cited for the high level of unemployment in Canada, and a number of recommendations to cope with the problem were enunciated, none more precisely than by the Leader of the Opposition Mr. Clark who opened the debate so eloquently this afternoon. Having listened to subsequent speeches, I find myself a bit appalled by the fact that no one has put a finger on the root of the reason for unemployment. The problem does not lie with the extension of the government's costly job creating programs, for example, because the majority of these programs do not solve the unemployment problem on a permanent basis; they give an appearance of assisting the situation on a temporary basis, when in fact in the long term they can simply be defined as phony.
The problem is not even with our large industries such as General Motors or Stelco where employment, in fact, has increased over the past years in accordance with the growth within their specific sectors. No, Mr. Speaker, this is not where the bulk of the labour force is and where the potential exists. Nor is the bulk comprised of the membership of the Canadian Labour Congress, for example. The majority of the labour force in Canada, and the greatest potential increase- this is backed by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce-are in the owner-managed sector of our economy, most often referred to as small and medium sized enterprises. Over 60 per cent of the labour force is employed either directly or indirectly by this vital sector. That sector is virtually ignored by this government and its philosophies of centralization. Oh yes, I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recently appointed my friend from Kamloops as the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand), but this move means absolutely nothing if the government's policies in gener-
[Mr. Jelinek.j
al are not altered in any way, shape or form, and this philosophy of centralization continues to exist.
One can only assume that the reason for forming this sub-ministry is simply a temporary move to pacify the disgruntled small businessman. If one looks back prior to the 1974 election and remembers a Ministry of Multiculturalism having been established, only to be quickly abolished after a Liberal mandate was assured, one could easily conclude that the same procedure may be followed in this instance and that the future of the Minister of State (Small Businesses) will not be long lived.
To illustrate a specific example, allow me to point out the plea of the small or specialty apparel shops, of which there are literally thousands in every part of the country. As a result of the blanket quotas on the imports of textiles imposed recently by the government, the majority of these small shopowners are being threatened with bankruptcy and are presently in the process of laying off perhaps tens of thousands of employees because they fall under this blanket quota program.
It is not because they are a threat to our own textile industry which, granted, deserves the protection it needs. The majority of these shops do not even attempt to compete with the large textile manufacturers such as Dupont and others, and must continue to be dependent on quotas which they may not even have had in 1975. Yet, when questioned just yesterday, the Minister of State (Small Businesses) was apparently so unconcerned with this situation, which falls directly within his jurisdiction, that he had not even approached the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) with representations as to the possibility of exempting the quotas within this important but harmless market.
This is only one typical example where government action is harmful to the small business community and results in a yet further deterioration in the employment situation. There are, in fact, countless examples of such instances all stemming from the fact, as I said earlier, of the government's insistence of continuing their philosophy of centralization and introduction of legislation for the benefit of big business without having had any consultation, or given any thought whatsoever to what consequences a small business will face.
It is of immense necessity that governments in general extend their consultations to the small firms sector and deal with that sector as a separate entity when developing policies and introducing legislation. The fact that the potential labour growth is within this small firms sector can no longer be ignored, and one must realize at the same time that the most economical form of employment opportunity lies with the entrepreneur who is constantly struggling to avoid the obstacles this government's actions cause to fall in his path.
Surely it would not be difficult for the government to reduce the tons of bureaucratic paperwork the small businessman is expected to cope with, including the total revamping of the costly tax structure as it relates to the small business community. Instead of strangling this community with bureaucracy
February 10, 1977

and all sorts of restrictions and controls, it is time that the government initiated forms of incentive, be they through the tax system, research and development, or what have you, incentives that would encourage the growth and development of the small firms thereby creating built-in employment at the lowest possible cost.
In any event, the fact of the matter remains that the largest economic growth potential is virtually at a standstill. Because it is in a stagnant position, the many jobs that could be generated from within this sector are simply non-existent. All of this is caused by the government's inability to come up with basic, long range policies. Instead, it governs on a day-to-day ad hoc basis causing an unprecedented climate of confusion and uncertainty within the economy as a whole. A businessman, be he involved in a large or small enterprise, simply cannot take the risk to expand or plan for the future knowing that the government may impose upon him overnight unexpected and impromptu changes, as it did with wage and price controls, for example.
There are many other areas that reflect on the unemployment figures that we, as Canadians, are faced with today, and they relate directly to the government's inability to deal with small and medium sized businesses in a realistic and businesslike fashion. However, with the time limitations that are imposed on us, I would like to introduce just one other area of potentially mammoth employment, related directly to the small and medium sized business sector. 1 am referring, of course, to secondary industry and secondary manufacturing.
In this regard I simply find it very difficult to comprehend the present situation in which we find ourselves. Canada, being one of the richest nations in natural resources, is at the bottom of the totem pole when it comes to secondary manufacturing. We encourage foreign interest to develop our natural resources, and to a certain extent this is a necessity, but then we fight like hell to sell our raw materials abroad where, as a result, jobs are created and economies bolstered. Then we purchase the finished goods in large quantities, goods that have been made out of our natural products in the first place, and we pay for them through the teeth without having reaped any advantages within our economy.
Needless to say, this trend that we have allowed to develop, and in fact encouraged, should and must be reversed if we are to reverse our sluggish economy and if we are to develop realistic long-range and permanent job opportunities. There are a number of ways this can be done, be it through various tax incentives or the availability to the entrepreneur of the vast technological research and development programs which the government is capable of having, but mainly it is the attitude and general philosophy of the government itself that has to be altered first.
We can no longer depend solely on the costly make-work programs which I alluded to earlier. They simply are not realistic and do not solve the underlying problems of unemployment. They are certainly not popular with the small businessman either. When the Canadian Federation of Independent Business asked their membership whether or not
Unemployment
they supported federal LIP programs as a way of providing direct employment, for example, only 16 per cent approved and over 65 per cent categorically did not. This poll was conducted on a national basis.
It is very clear that socialistically oriented programs tend to postpone the inevitable, and we are currently witnessing this inevitability. Therefore, if we want our country to remain the great place that it is, we must revert to the basic philosophies that it was built on, and I am of course referring to the freedom and encouragement of a successful free enterprise system, a system that must be maintained in its original form.

Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) this afternoon, I wondered whether they were talking about the same country. Indeed I wondered if they were talking about the same world. The Minister of Finance talked about this government transferring more than $2 billion to the taxpayers of Canada so that they could better meet their costs, and how they had increased old age pensions by $390 million. He told us that those who were unemployed received among the highest benefits in the world, and so on.
Then the minister said they could agree with everything which was in the motion and in the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) with one small exception, because the government had already done those things. What the minister forgot to tell us was that the number of those presently unemployed is higher than it has ever been since Statistics Canada began to collect these figures.
I listened to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. He began by telling us the government was not satisfied with the situation, and that as long as there was one unemployed person who wanted to work it would not be satisfied. He went on to recount all the good things it had done. He said our social programs are among the best in the world, and then he gave examples of programs it had introduced and which had created work, he said, in Montreal, Moncton, Saint John, and so on. Well, just a few days ago the unemployment figures for the month of January came out. How did the Toronto Globe and Mail report those figures? The headline on February 9 read: "889,000 Unemployed in January-Highest Total on Record".
The news story began:
Unemployment in January was 889,000, the highest recorded since monthly labour statistics began to be collected in 1953, Statistics Canada reports.
Since they concern the subject we are discussing today I think these figures ought to be put on record in relation to the speeches-the cynical speeches in my view-made by the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. There were 889,000 people unemployed last month, representing an increase over the same month in 1976 of 89,000.

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
What was the number of unemployed by regions in unadjusted figures? In the Atlantic provinces it was 105,000; in Quebec, 274,000, up 32,000 over the same month in 1976. Look at the rates. In the Atlantic region the unadjusted unemployment rate was 13.6 per cent. In recent weeks we have been discussing whether the figures are correct or not. I do not think anybody but one or two cabinet ministers would deny that there are thousands of people presently unemployed who are not counted in the statistics. There are a number of reasons for this. They might have been unemployed for longer than the period during which they are included in statistics. They might be young people who have never held a job. They might be single wage or salary earners who feel that unemployment in their areas is so high there is no use registering for work.
In Quebec there were 274,000 unemployed in January, and the unadjusted unemployment rate was 10.3 per cent. I am not so naive as to think the only reason some people in Quebec believe in a separate state is because they are hungry or because they are unemployed. I recognize there are linguistic, cultural or historical reasons why some people there have come to believe in a separate state. I do not believe that all the 40 per cent of the people of Quebec who voted for the Parti Quebecois were voting for a separate state, but I suggest to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that the 274,000 people who are unemployed in the province-I suppose if you look at Quebec east of Montreal you are looking at an unemployment rate not of 10 per cent but of between 12 and 14 per cent, and in the Gaspe you are talking about a rate of 30 or 40 per cent-could be forgiven if they are not enthused by the concept of one Canada. I am surprised there are not more who have been turned off in their thinking about Canada.
I suggest to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce that what we do not need are ringing platitudes about his belief in one Canada. What we do need is a belief on the part of the federal government that Canada can have full employment. It is thinking of that kind which could lead Quebec and other regions to believe that Canada as a country means something.
We have heard ad nauseam from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) that the unemployment figures are not as serious as they sound, because among the people they include are many women seeking to earn second incomes. Then we hear the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) saying recently that women should not be working. Again, it is said there are a lot of young people who really do not want to work and who try to get by on unemployment insurance. Well, the recent survey by Statistics Canada which showed there were 889,000 unemployed tells us two-fifths of them were heads of families or single people living alone. The bureau's own figures suggest that the additional number of workers available for work but not counted could amount to anywhere between 108,000 and 573,000 during January, depending upon the criteria used.

What I am saying now is what this party has been saying for a considerable time. We are in a major crisis, and it is only the government which refuses to face the fact.
What are the prospects for 1977? I refer hon. members to a survey recently carried out by the Conference Board, a very respected organization which conducts economic surveys, and whose membership includes academics, business people and a few labour people. The result of that study is reported in a recent issue of the Globe and Mail as follows:
Canadian economic growth will slow markedly in 1977 with real gross national product expanding only 3 per cent compared with nearly 5 per cent this year, the Conference Board in Canada estimates.
The prospects for 1977 have deteriorated because of the unanticipated continuation of the weak economic recovery in the major industrialized countries, particularly the United States, which are Canada's trading partners.
A slow-down in the growth of the GNP means more unemployment in 1977 than in 1976. The Financial Times, again not a very radical or revolutionary journal of opinion, said in a recent editorial:
Canada's economy should have produced 87,000 more jobs than it has since May, 1975-the bottom of the recession-in order to have made any inroads into the number of unemployed.
The outlook for unemployment is expected to worsen in Canada this year, especially without any fiscal stimulation. From Plains, Ga., president-elect Jimmy Carter has already shot his $15 billion fiscal bolt, largely directed at creating jobs in the U.S.
The article goes on to point out that even if Canada had that kind of program, which it has not, it would not mean a very drastic cut in the rate of unemployment we are presently facing. If we believe that this country could have full employment and that the bulk of our people who are now unemployed really want to work-

speechtext:
If we believe, Mr. Speaker, that it is better for people who are now unemployed to be working than to live off unemployment insurance benefits or welfare of various types, then we must ask ourselves how we can put our unemployed to work. It seems to me that we have only two possibilities which, pursued separately or together, are these: either the private sector of the economy will expand and hire a substantial portion of the tens of thousands who are unemployed, or in the public sector the federal, provincial and municipal governments will activate programs that will employ people.
Let me examine the private sector and ask whether it will fill the need and hire a substantial percentage, I will not say all, of the 889,000 people who are now unemployed according to Statistics Canada. It is obvious that the demand for products produced by Canadian companies, by the private sector of the Canadian economy, is not there. Manufacturing capacity
February 10, 1977

is now operating at only 85 per cent of capacity. This means that whatever tax incentives the government proposes in its wisdom two or three months from now, or whenever it is the Minister of Finance brings forward his budget, they will not in fact do the job. The C. D. Howe Research Institute, in examining the result we might get from further tax concessions, said that these "are unlikely to be the major determinant of investment; business perceptions of the future prospects for the economy are likely to be the critical factor in investment decisions".
That being the case, Mr. Speaker, it is not likely that companies that are not now working at full capacity will be hiring any substantial number of people. With close to one million unemployed we are losing in the neighbourhood of between $5 billion and $6 billion worth of production each year. It seems to me that if the private sector is not in a position to hire people-I do not say that in any critical sense; it will hire people when there is demand for its products-then there is only one alternative, and that is government action.
We have proposed today in the form of an amendment to the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) five specific methods for dealing with unemployment. The first proposal is for an immediate decrease in personal income taxes for those in the lower and middle income groups, for the purpose of stimulating their purchasing power, and to help take up the current slack in the economy.
The Minister of Finance claims that the government has already done this through its indexation of income tax. I do not have the time today to put on the record again what we have done many times to show that the bulk of benefits derived from indexing income tax goes to those in the middle and upper income brackets. They are people who can afford to save. They are people who do not spend all the money they get back as a result of tax cuts.
I should like to compare our indexing proposals with that which President Carter has proposed in the United States. He is proposing an immediate tax credit of $50 for every taxpayer in the United States. The bulk of this money will go to people in the low income brackets who will spend it because they find it difficult to meet the rapidly increasing cost of living in the United States. We suggest to the government that that kind of proposal should be put into effect in Canada immediately. People should be given the opportunity to take the credit, not on their 1977 income but on their 1976 income, when they prepare their 1976 income tax return.
We have also suggested that there should be an immediate reactivation of all federal capital works projects, not just those of the federal government, and we should encourage the provinces and municipalities to follow suit, at the same time lifting any restraint on their share of funding such projects.
Let me give the House an example which I gave before the Olympics were held. I thought then, and still think, that it was madness to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on a two week extravaganza in a city of two and a half million people which is still dumping its raw sewage into the St. Lawrence river. The city has plans that are ready for a sewage treatment
Unemployment
plant, but it has had to delay the implementation of those plans because it has borrowed so much money for the Olympics that it does not have any credit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a debate like this one, it is natural for the opposition to try to depict the employment situation in Canada under a certain lighting. I did say "lighting" because, as a matter of fact, we were rather offered a great "blackness" with these fireworks of questionable of "Broadbentic" statistics, or others.
I do not intend to minimize the gravity of the situation but I would like to recall, as the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) did this afternoon, that the unemployment problem should be considered in its real context. However, this phenomenon is not limited to Canada. All the large industrial countries, including the United States where President Carter is going to implement a special program in this area, have to face a similar situation. Indeed, as far as statistics are concerned, ours as published each month by Statistics Canada are more complete with their distribution by region, by class of workers or by age group. In most countries, where there are several different schemes they are instruments which could not be rigorously accurate. It is understandable because we know that tens of thousands of Canadians shift from one job to another every week and it is, of course, a sample. But because of such estimates we can provide our job creation programs with better accuracy so as to allow further consideration to the needs of specific regions such as the province of Quebec and the Maritimes.
This kind of barometer also allows for better appraising of the impact of some programs and thus enabled us to realize that in January in the province of Quebec, because of the efforts made by the federal government through its public works and its job creation programs, the situation had improved and there were 20,000 fewer unemployed. It does not change the situation for those Canadians who are out of work but the program which I will refer to in a few moments and which has been specifically designed for that purpose will look after this situation.
Mr. Speaker, the number of Canadians who are working and the standard of living of the Canadian people, including those who are having problems, have never been so high. There are countries which do not have statistics on unemployment; would Canadians accept this other formula which indeed denies the word accept itself. There are also other formulas La Presse editorialist Ivan Guay pointed out last January 12 how some policies of the Labour Party which were often praised in this House had led Great Britain to its present economic difficulties. I was in England last September and I also found out that although there was a rate of inflation of 13.5 per cent, the unions of that country were allowing that workers be

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
granted increases of about 4.5 per cent. They were accepting 4.5 per cent in order to settle agreements. But here, how much criticism we got, especially from the official opposition, when in our current anti-inflation programs the increases granted are always higher while inflation still exists.
Magic remedies and final solutions lie nowhere on our planet, and the global effort the government of Canada is making this year has no equivalent with its programs whose efficiency has already been proven, and other programs which are ahead of what is done throughout the world; many countries are indeed on their way to adapt them, such as LIP. But in Canada, we are ahead of our time with programs like "Canada Works" and "Young Canada Works", which I will discuss in a moment. That does not consider the regional assistance nor the considerable amounts made available to the provinces through equalization which next year will provide the provinces for instance with $2.5 billion, including $1.3 billion to Quebec.
Here again, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to hon. members' attention what must exist between provincial government and the federal government, and in particular the Quebec government. Very recently, in the Ottawa Journal of last February 9, we read that the mayor of Hull is very much worried about the existing situation, and I quote:

Taking into account that each worker spends on average $800 a year in the place he works, Mr. Rocheleau says that one building alone with 5,000 employees would mean $4 million being spent in the area nearby.

The mayor is worried over the fact that projects amounting to $26 million could be cancelled, just because of a policy which would be rather difficult to understand for the Quebec government. Just as he does I wish the new Minister for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) could meet them to correct the situation in which they seem to get in.
Mr. Speaker, 1 was just referring to the Local Initiatives Program, a program which allows enormous sums of money to be pumped into the economy where the situation is most serious. For this winter we have a program worth about $200 million which will create 47,000 jobs, about one third of them in Quebec. Furthermore, we are presently completing the allocation of $60 million for Phase I of Canada Works program. There will be $140 million more in this sector by the end of this fiscal year, which will allow for the creation of a total of 61,000 jobs.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote some figures dated February 8, 1977 which show the interest of most Canadians looking for employment and the groups which would like to co-operate with the new Canada Works project. We note that on February 8, 1977, there was 6,630 applications to create about 62,000 jobs representing $340 million. This shows the interest of some people in creating employment in Canada. I agree with the leader of the NDP. We know that Canadians are not lazy and that they would rather work than receive unemployment insurance benefits or social welfare allowances.

I do not feel however that programs such as Canada Works or the Local Initiatives Program are a form of social assistance. I am sure of that in my constituency, because I have some evidence that the people who are now interested in various LIP projects are eager to work and willing to help. Nor only do they earn a salary, but their work has a social aspect. In most cases, they help senior citizens, visiting them at home once or twice a week, to do their housework and other things. What those women do in those programs is desirable, and I trust that in the not too distant future the provinces will give similar home services to the needy. Once again, the federal government will have taken an initiative which can perhaps be followed up by federal-provincial agreements.
In all its programs the government has given special attention to the young, helping them either to complete their studies or to have easier access to the labour market. For instance, in the next few months, thanks to three programs, namely Young Canada Works, the Summer Job Corps and summer jobs in various federal departments, 47,000 jobs will be created, at a cost of $65 million. The program Young Canada alone will allow expenditures of $26 million. The number of manpower centres on Canadian campuses will increase from 70 to 88 across Canada in the next three years.
Another program will exist after Bill C-27 has been studied. I trust the House will pass it fairly quickly. With the integration of the two departments, the Department of Manpower still has a very interesting program in co-operative education. A budget already set at $500,000 will enable the federal government, and those provincial governments that are interested, to cooperate in looking for a solution to what I feel is a major problem so that students, while taking classes, can spend some time in private industry; this training period can serve as a bridge between studies and a job. Too often, when applying for a job, young people with 12 or 15 years of schooling are asked whether they have some experience. Unfortunately, they are unable to say that they have some and their application is turned down. I think that a thorough study of the matter with the funds made available after the creation of the new department could probably solve one of the major problems. Perhaps this will answer the question put today by the leader of the opposition when he referred to the father who was rather disappointed because his children who were graduates found it difficult to land a job. The educational system should also provide courses for which there are openings so that the young people will not realize, once they have completed their studies, that there is no employment for them.
In addition, young people and other groups of workers can take advantage of a massive operation whose full extent I have been in a position to evaluate as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration; the training or retraining programs for workers in institutions as well as in industry.
Mr. Speaker, in 1976-77, the department is going to spend $477 million for institutional training and $64 million for
February 10, 1977

on-the-job training, a total of $541 million. In 1977-78, within two months from now, the Department of Manpower and Immigration is going to increase its spendings in this field, allocating $513 million for institutional training and $70 million for on-the-job training or a total of $583 million. This is to help Canadians improve their skill and find a job.
Indeed, not only will these investments increase the qualifications of the Canadian workers and allow them to find a job more easily instead of receiving unemployment insurance benefits but they will also help them take a more active part in the economy of our country. I could talk about many other programs to help the disabled workers who need special training. For example, there is the LIAP-Local Improvement Assistance Program-which, with $14.8 million, will create this year 18,840 man-months. In our department, we have, among others, the workers' mobility program.
Mr. Speaker, if I have enough time, I would like to point out other innovations in a bill now before the House and which will be applied if the Department of Manpower and the Unemployment Insurance Commission can better coordinate their operations once they will be merged. I hope I can deal more deeply with this subject when we will study the bill, but right now I want to tell you how the work sharing program will be applied. Beginning next fiscal year, it will help avoid lay-offs in factories or industries with temporary problems.
Usually, we cut down on personnel, which creates unemployment and results in a loss of skilled staff for a company. This work-sharing program will help keep the whole personnel, but the work week will be temporarily reduced and the cost will be charged to the new Employment and Immigration Commission. These are pilot projects which will come into effect next fall in an effort to improve the condition of the workers who have difficulties and help them keep their incomes. This will be done as generously and cautiously as possible.
This formula brought positive results in several industrialized countries, especially the German Federal Republic and its cost is partly balanced by the unemployment insurance spendings which could not otherwise be avoided. Obviously the elaboration of such a program is complicated and cooperation will be expected not only from governments, and employers but from workers and their unions as well. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) indicated recently that there was a danger that the employers might be tempted to abuse the system and make it absorb some of their losses. I agree that we will have to proceed with care but if we doubt the good faith of those who are ready to participate in such a program, we would never have had programs such as local Initiatives, training on the job, Canada Works, Young Canada Works, etc. Of course the opposition would be in a better position then to criticize the government and produce fine statistics.
Mr. Speaker, the new job creation strategy announced recently by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration includes a new formula which will allow this year a pilot project for the unemployed which will encourage them to
Unemployment
participate voluntarily in projects of direct job creation within the community and still receive their unemployment insurance benefits. Or still, again on a voluntary basis, to take training courses while their benefits continue to be their main source of income. It will be suggested that in certain cases the benefits are higher than the salaries being offered. Those are rare cases, and the formula is intended particularly to help those who are thinking about improving their skills while they are waiting to find a job, therefore improving their chances of finding a job, and also keeping more busy in an interim period which they want to be as short as possible.
In brief, Mr. Speaker, we are in the presence of an additional effort by the government which all told is going to cost over $1 billion to bring unemployment across Canada to its lowest level possible with special attention going to those areas where the situation is more difficult. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I still want to note certain points raised by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) who seems to be extremely concerned with small business or at least certain small businesses. I would indeed like him to define them. If it is about certain storekeepers that he is concerned, I hope that in his case there is no conflict of interest.
I have here an item made in Hong Kong bearing the name Jelinek Import Registered. This may not be one of his companies or the company of one of his relatives but it is still the same name. The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) was also in agreement with the positions taken by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and, as he suggested this afternoon, bringing imports from Asia and elsewhere back to the rate of 1975 helps to create more jobs in Canada.
That is the main objective. In my area and in Quebec as well as outside thousands of textile workers are losing their jobs because of continued imports of all sorts of clothing made outside this country. 1 think they should rather buy Canadian to create thousands of jobs in Canada and not import or be afraid that some imports will not come in. There is not a dealer handling 100 per cent imports. In the majority of cases they have Canadian products, for sure.
And even they are permitted to import 75 per cent of the current quota. I think it is enough to continue to create jobs here, and that would not be one of my main fears. I think the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is simply doing its job, and it certainly has the support of the majority of government members.
