speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the opportunity to say a few words on the motion moved by my leader this afternoon:
That this House denounces the government's failure to generate jobs in Canada, particularly in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, and urges immediate and resolute action, including the early presentation of a budget.
I listened very carefully to the speech of our leader which, I thought, was a reasoned one and contained very good suggestions. It was well presented. I also listened to the speech of the

February 10, 1977
Unemployment
leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent), which similarly was good. However, I regretted his attitude at one point. For a while I even thought we were in government because he was attacking the Conservative party so much. However, I suppose that if, for 30 or 40 years, you cannot change the polls or win an election you have to lash out in every direction. Nevertheless, on one point I do agree with the Leader of the NDP, contrary to what the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) said, namely, that there are more than 889,000 people unemployed in this country. The minister better realize that day after day members from the Atlantic provinces and from Quebec are in constant contact with people they represent. They receive letters from them saying, "Look, I have to get a job. You say, "Go to Manpower". Look, I am tired of going to Manpower. I've been going there for months and I cannot find any work there". This is not the fault of the officials in the Manpower offices. They do not have any work to give anyone. Let me give you an example.
The following is the type of letter I get from my constituents:
Dear Sir:
This is the first time that I have written to any MP. I guess there is a first time for everything.
The reason that I am writing is to get a little information to help plan my future. Just maybe you can help.
I am a widower, with three small children. I have worked every day since I got out of school. I was laid off at SYSCO ten weeks ago. 1 was wondering if you could advise me on my next move. I have been going around looking for work but there is none to be found. I love working; it keeps my mind off things. Do you think I should stay around and wait to sec what happens at SYSCO or should I pull up roots and go west to look for work?
1 have lived all my life in Sydney and I don't want to leave and I don't want to go on welfare. Do you think something will break soon?
Keep up the good work and keep fighting for the working man. May the Lord be in your corner.
This is the type of letter we get, time and time again, from many people who cannot find jobs. The thesis put forward by the Leader of the NDP is not new. I have stated it in the House before. I have also said it outside the House and I say now that the figures we get are not legitimate. There are thousands of people who are not classified as being unemployed in the Manpower offices, therefore they are not considered to be out of a job. So the figures we get are phony. There are over 1 million unemployed in this country. I say that to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who has become arrogant when anyone asks him a question about the unemployed in this country. He used to be a regular, fine, decent gentleman. I think he better watch out and take lessons from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) who knows how to answer people in the House and who does not get carried away by the importance of his position. We can do without his arrogance. It does not help the unemployed.
As my leader said, eight out of every ten Canadians joined the ranks of the unemployed from the five eastern provinces. These are not bodies, as referred to in bureaucratic language, they are not just figures or statistics, they are human beings.

All we heard this afternoon was statistics. All the last speaker gave us was statistics. All we heard from the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, and from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) was statistics. But they do not pay the rent, they do not pay the mortgage, they do not buy the food, and they do not buy clothes for the kids.
Before I go any further I want to say a word about Quebec, La Belle Province. The good people of that province are not interested in separatism. They are not one bit interested in moving away from Canada. What they want is an economic climate in which they can make a buck. That green stuff talks. What is the use of being able to speak two, three or four languages if you cannot find a job? If we provide the proper economic climate-and the government should provide that climate-we will not hear very much about separatism in the province of Quebec.
On several occasions the Minister of Finance expressed his serious concern about the unemployment situation, and I believe him. He talks about job creation, but since December, 1976, he tells us that there have been only 79,000 new jobs created. What the hell is the good of 79,000 new jobs when over one million are unemployed? I know it has helped a little bit, but it is still not the answer.
The minister is the bantam rooster type. Although he is not small, he is ready for a fight. However, he condescended to say that the leader of our party and the leader of the New Democratic Party put forward some good suggestions, and that he would keep them in mind when he is proposing a budget a few months hence.

speechtext:
That is quite right. I go along with one point in the amendment proposed by the New Democratic Party. In fact I go along with all of them. I go along with co-operative housing in Nova Scotia. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has been down there. The former minister, the minister who is now looking after the Boy Scouts of Canada, our last line of defence, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), was down there talking about a cooperative program in Nova Scotia which would provide jobs. He is doing nothing about it and has done nothing about it. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) talks about grants and about all the jobs they produce, but they are not producing jobs in the Atlantic provinces. I do not know where they are producing jobs.
One of the factors which has affected the employment situation in Cape Breton in the last couple of years has been a strike at Nova Scotia Forest Industries, which affected 1,500 employees. That was a legitimate strike. The company was trying to get the employees to work for nothing. The Cape Breton construction industry is down to its lowest ebb in years, creating more unemployment, because of the economic climate in this country. Construction employment at the heavy water
February 10, 1977

plant has wound down. There was a disastrous fire at Devco's No. 26 colliery, which put more people out of work. There has been a softening of demand in the world steel markets. At Canadian Motor Industries we used to assemble Toyota cars, but that effort has gone down the drain. They have pulled out. 1 raised this matter time and time again with the then minister of industry, trade and commerce, but there were no results. Nothing happened. Forty of the boys who were laid off got together and borrowed $3,000 apiece and set up a fund of $120,000 to try to do something themselves with other agencies, but there was no co-operation either from the provincial or federal governments.
General Instruments employed 1,000 people assembling tuners for car radios and so on, but it is gone. There was no effort made by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to keep that company there. The Kaiser strontium plant is going out of business. Just today the Nova Scotia development minister said that the province could not buy or subsidize this plant. That means 100 more people out of work. I tried to make contact with the Asahi Glass Company in Tokyo. What has Devco done about that? What has the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce done to get them interested in taking over this plant? Nothing.
In the last two years 1,664 men have been laid off by the SYSCO steel plant, the Sidney Steel Corporation. Today, when I checked the number on the payroll at SYSCO, it was 2,290. Two years ago it was 3,954. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce mentioned me in dispatches several times today during his speech that I was always raising hell and crying for more rail orders, etc. Why would I not, when we have all these steelworkers walking the streets, losing their houses, being put out into the cold, and unable to pay their electric bills because the power rates are so high?
The minister also said I have been after him about decentralization. Of course I have. Let us move a government department down to Cape Breton. That would provide 800 or 900 jobs. The lame excuse of the minister was that some members in this party did not think it would be a good idea. That is not the point at all. The minister misled the House because the members of this party, as well as the mayor of Ottawa, said that they want a program and that they want to know what is going to happen. Is there going to be an announcement tomorrow that some department is moving? We want to know ahead of time. The minister promised that there would be an outline right after Christmas, but it has not come yet. I would like to see a department brought down there so that people in that area can be employed. Let us not move people just for the sake of moving them. The Department of Veterans Affairs is moving to P.E.I., but that will not be for another three years. It might be like the causeway the Liberal Government was going to build to P.E.I.; it never did come about; perhaps the move of the Department of Veterans Affairs will not, either.

Of course the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, in addition to negotiating with New Brunswick, negotiates continuously with Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland with regard to federal-provincial agreements. They bring millions of dollars to create new jobs, develop the highway structure so that the economy can be

improved, and assist in the development of the tourist trade of the Atlantic provinces.

The decentralization approach which the government has taken, one area of activity with regard to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, is revealed most markedly in the administration of the Regional Development Incentives Act. Provincial directors general now decide on cases involving up to $500,000 in capital costs and 40 jobs, while regional assistant deputy ministers are authorized to approve all cases involving capital costs of between $500,000 and $1.5 million and up to 100 jobs. There is greater co-operation than ever before between the two levels of government on the matter of incentives to industry. This is the type of positive approach that the government takes in co-operating with those provinces.

He tells the Canadian people he would like to remain as Leader of the Official Opposition. In his travels across the country, he talks about how he will do this and that, and what a great future there will be. However, he does not seem to have the capacity or ability to put on record exactly what his position is with regard to the very difficult problems which face us today.
The Canadian people will be watching the performance of the opposition very closely. We hear them continuously moan, cry, and lament. It will not be surprising to see them remain in that position for another ten or 15 years, as has been the case for the last number of years. When you consider their performance and input in this House, you observe almost a non-opposition situation. They say nothing constructive. Mr. Speaker, I am very dismayed that we on this side of the House were obliged to bring in a motion today in order to focus attention on what I call a national disaster, that is, high unemployment. The last speaker talked about decisive leadership. All I can say is that at this time in our history we Find there are increasing numbers of our youth who feel alienated, increasing numbers who are prepared to work but are unable to do so because of incompetence in the management of the economy. We have not found jobs for our youth.
When the hon. member refers to decisive leadership, I think of the senior citizen who is frustrated and who feels that we, as parliamentarians, do not realize the presence within that group of a bank of skilled resources from which there have not been sufficient withdrawals, that the government has no idea of what these people could do in terms of bringing about a better climate in terms of the economic situation. They have been put out to pasture. That is the kind of decisive leadership the hon. member was talking about. He continually forgets that business is suspicious. CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-COMMUTER SERVICE IN MONTREAL AREA-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the constituency of Vaudreuil includes the Canadian Pacific Railway commuter passenger train service that runs from Rigaud through Hudson, Vaudreuil, lie Perrot, Ste. Annes, Baie d'Urfe and Beaconsfield, into Montreal. A total of about 7,500 passengers use this line each day on which there are a total of 26 stops. The annual loss is over $300 per passenger.
The announcement of the CPR in January of fare increases, coupled with drastic cuts in the number of trains, was followed by some 40 letters to me from individuals and municipalities requesting federal intervention to stop the reduction in service.
Most of the complaints relate to the reduction in trains between Vaudreuil and Rigaud. About 400 passengers a day use this section of the line. In such a situation one does not First argue jurisdictional responsibilities, so on Thursday of last week I proposed a motion which can be found on page 2667 of Hansard. It reads:
That the Minister of Transport personally intervene on behalf of all the commuters in the Montreal area and solicit from CPR a postponement of its intention to reduce the frequency of service until the province of Quebec indicates its policy on or before July 1.
The request for the postponement is related to the urban transportation study by the province of Quebec which is expected on or before July 1 of this year.
In recent months the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has intervened to obtain a delay in the introduction of fare and service changes for the Montreal commuter rail services announced by CNR and CPR. The minister has indicated that the Financial support of these services is the responsibility of the province of Quebec, and his intervention has been taken to minimize inconvenience to the public until the provincial government has determined how it will exercise its responsibility.
Although it is acknowledged that the provision of urban transportation services is the responsibility of municipal and provincial governments, which should also take responsibility for the costs, a federal program of capital assistance can help in relieving problems by providing capital to assist in the expansion of public urban transportation services.
I recognize that any federal urban transportation assistance program is not likely to subsidize the operation of urban commuter and transit systems. Nevertheless, this government has made a commitment to provide assistance to urban areas in order to alleviate their transportation problems. The promise of this financial assistance, and the role played by the federally appointed Canadian Transport Commission, led to the public appeal to the federal government.
I appreciate the prompt action of the Minister of Transport. Many residents in the constituency of Vaudreuil are entirely dependent upon public transportation, and service cuts of the magnitude of those announced by CPR would impose considerable hardships on those people who, for a multitude of reasons, do not have the use of a private automobile.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I on appropriate occasions in the past have made numerous representations to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) regarding the unacceptably high level of cheese imports.

February 10, 1977
Adjournment Debate
On January 25, 1977, I asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to clarify press reports attributed to the chairman of the Canadian Dairy Commission to the effect that the freeze on cheese imports imposed a year ago would be extended for an additional year. I also asked the minister if he would not consider using a well accepted government practice of utilizing a previous five-year averaging approach in establishing a more acceptable and equitable basis for cheese import levels. If such a principle were to be adopted, our cheese import level would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of 38 million or 40 million pounds.
Replying in the usual fine tradition of his cabinet colleagues, the minister said in part that he would inquire. It is widely known and recognized throughout the industry that, although naturally not accepted by the government, the decision to freeze import cheese levels at 50 million pounds a year ago was largely, if not entirely, the result of opposition protests, protests which were raised here in this House on this side of the House.
Concern about this problem is the result of a number of factors. When the quota on cheese imports was first set by the government in 1975, it was established at too high a level. Imports of variety cheese in 1973 and 1974 were 38 million pounds and 45 million pounds respectively. If a significant portion of such imports had not been subsidized by the countries of origin, the volume experienced in the two years prior to the application of the quota would never have been achieved.
Second, in 1974 it is common knowledge that greater volumes entered Canada illegally because of inadequate policing methods, and further to that, no action was taken except to legalize the entry.
Third, another case in point involves cheese believed to be from East Germany which is trans-shipped via West Germany and enters our market at the level of 56 cents a pound. This transshipment situation was never proved; however, there is no way West Germany could sell cheese at 56 cents a pound when the Common Market support prices are close to a dollar.
Yet another factor which discredits the use of 1974 cheese levels as a standard is the fact that more cheese was imported due to a shortage of Canadian milk that particular year. The government failed to take into account that commencing in 1972 Canada's trade in cheese had become totally imbalanced, largely because of the trade protection measures imposed by the European Economic Community, whose member countries enjoy some 65 per cent of the share of the expanding cheese trade into Canada.
Our cheese exports, which traditionally have been dominated by sales to the United Kingdom, fell from the 30 million pound level in 1970 and 1971 to 18 million pounds in 1972 and to 6 million pounds in 1973. Since then they have amounted to less than three million or four million pounds.
In contrast, cheese imports, mainly from the trading bloc which has wiped out our traditional export market, have nearly doubled, from some 20 million pounds in 1970 to probably close to 50 million pounds in 1976.

When the loss of cheese exports is combined with the growth of cheese imports over the past five years, the Canadian dairy industry has lost a potential market for half a billion pounds of industrial milk, or about 5 per cent of total requirements.
Every ten million pounds of cheese imported into Canada cost the Canadian dairy industry approximately $4 million. It should not have come as any surprise to the federal government under these circumstances that the dairy industry strongly opposed the establishment of the quota level at 50 million pounds in the past two years. The government failed to recognize that the Canadian dairy industry is quite capable of producing nearly all the varieties of cheese that are being imported into this country. The government has implied that this is not possible, and that consumers must be able to purchase the cheese of their choice. I wish to lay this myth to rest once and for all. It should be noted as well that savings on lower cost cheese imports are not passed on in the same relative proportions to the consumer.
In the first place, the Canadian industry manufactured and offered for sale to the public, some 50 different varieties of cheese in 1975, many of which are the exact same varieties being imported. Second, about a dozen specialty cheeses which together make up about half the imported varieties in tonnage, either are or can be manufactured in Canada without difficulty.
It is nonsense to suggest that Canada requires the imported cheeses because of our inability to make them. The real problem is the government's lack of policy to prevent imports from being subsidized by the countries of origin. The effect of this is that the Canadian manufacturers have no incentive to invest in plant and equipment to manufacture some of the large volume import varieties here.
I would like to point out that a ten million pound reduction in cheese imports would generate some $20 million or more of sales for the domestic industry, while at the same time saving skim milk powder export costs of close to $5 million.
It should be noted, as well, that the special access agreement for mature Canadian cheddar which Canada worked out with the EEC in early 1975, and which the government announced with considerable satisfaction, is in today's environment practically worthless. It is high time for the government to review this access agreement and either improve it or put more restrictions on cheese imports from EEC countries to Canada.
I would suggest that the responsibility for the control of all dairy products should rest with the Canadian Dairy Commission, which already manages dairy product export operations. It controls butter imports and has a vital over-all co-ordination role to play in carrying out federal government dairy policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with pleasure this evening to correct the unfounded and misleading statements which the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) made in this House on January 25, 1977.
I should like to begin by advising hon. members that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has never proposed that the cheese import quota should be doubled. The global cheese import quota was first implemented in Canada in 1975 in support of the domestic supply-management program for industrial milk. Prior to this date, there was no limitation on the quantity of cheese which could be imported into this country. The government took this action under Article 11, section 2 subsection (c) of the GATT which permits the implementation of import restrictions in support of supply management programs. The maximum import level for all types of cheeses was maintained at 50 million pounds for 1976-77, and the Minister of Agriculture has already indicated on numerous occasions that this level will not be increased for the 1977-78 dairy year.
It should be noted that under this quota imports of cheddar cheese are limited to a maximum of one million pounds. The other 49 million pounds represent specialty cheeses. The market for these cheeses has increased rapidly in Canada in recent years to the point where it is now economically feasible for Canadian cheese manufacturers to produce some 60 varieties. However, Canada continues to import some 200 cheese varieties, the market of which for many of these does not justify their production in Canada. Hopefully, with increased consumption of these varieties, it will become economically feasible to produce them in Canada, as has happened with numerous other varieties of specialty cheeses.
The maintenance of the quota of 50 million pounds has permitted the domestic industry to absorb growth in the market such that the cheese sector accounted for some 31 million hundredweights of milk, or 30 per cent of the industrial milk supply in 1976, compared with 29 million hundredweights, or 27 per cent of industrial milk supply in 1975.
Rather than restricting opportunity in the Canadian cheese industry, the limit on imports has permitted it to look to the future with confidence.

In the first place, we have provided a special allowance for status Indians living on reserves and on Crown lands. Indeed, since they are not included in the inquiry on people at work made by Statistics Canada and that they will probably not be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, they would not otherwise be taken into consideration in the basic allocation of funds.
Likewise, we do not grant special allowances to status Indians nor to the Metis people who do not live on reserves, because they are not included in the inquiry on people at work. In addition, if we do not receive enough reasonable suggestions from Indians living on reserves

More precisely, about the electoral district of Winnipeg North, Mr. Speaker, I would add that the rate of surplus manpower is 6.01 per cent. Regular allowance amounted to $100,000. Since the riding does not include status Indians living on reserves nor on Crown lands, it has not received the special allowance that was intended.

If, in the electoral district of Winnipeg North, the natives living in cities represent a group where unemployment is high, I am sure the advisory commission will give them priority; further, considering the allowance made to Winnipeg North, I am convinced that the natives' needs will be met satisfactorily.
